sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-SME-PD-2026.1 used for the development, calibration and testing of the PD Retail SME model version 2.0 (model identifier MDL-04), the gradient boosting rating system that assigns 12-month PDs to the Bank's retail SME exposures under the A-IRB approach. The range of application comprises retail exposures to self-employed natural persons (sole proprietors), partnerships and legal entities that qualify as SMEs, whose total amount owed by the group of connected clients does not exceed EUR 1 million and which are managed as part of a pool of exposures with similar characteristics, as required for the retail exposure class under CRR Art. 123 and 147(5). Products in scope are business current account credit lines, business term loans, owner-occupied business mortgage loans and business credit cards booked by the Bank's Dutch business banking entity; leasing and factoring exposures are booked in other Group entities and are outside the range of application. The RDS serves three uses: risk differentiation (training and testing of the ranking model), risk quantification (calibration of grade PDs to the long-run average default rate) and the quantification of the margin of conservatism. The document follows the RDS template of Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0; sections added to the template (for example 2.3, 2.4, 3.5 and 5.4) are numbered after the last template section of the relevant chapter so that the template numbering is preserved.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains 52 quarterly reference dates from 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2024, each followed by a 12-month outcome window, so that default outcomes are observed until 31 December 2025. It holds 5,184,312 obligor-quarter observations of 214,580 unique obligors with 402,910 unique facilities, 27,940 default events after the linking of multiple defaults, and 104,215 observations with a default in the 12-month outcome window (2.01%). The unit of observation is the non-defaulted obligor at a reference date; on average 99,700 obligors are observed per reference date, rising from 86,400 in 2012 to 111,900 in 2024. The default proportion of the development sample (2.12%) is higher than the one-year default rate of the application portfolio at reference date 30 June 2025 (1.61%); the difference reflects the inclusion of the 2012–2014 recession years and is documented in section 5.1.1.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts at 31 March 2012, the first quarter-end after the migration of business banking accounts from the legacy system BBS to CoreBank SME in 2011; obligor-level limit, arrears and transaction histories before that date were not migrated and cannot be linked to the current party identifiers. All relevant internal data after the migration are used, so the observation period is a continuous span of 14 default years that includes the five most recent years and extends well beyond them. The window covers the 2012–2013 Dutch recession, with the highest number of business bankruptcies since 1981, the recovery years 2014–2019, the COVID-19 period with government support measures in 2020–2021 and the energy price and inflation shock of 2022–2023, and therefore contains a mix of good and bad years including a downturn. The historical data required for the estimation, including rating histories, default events and exposure histories since 2012, are retained in the Risk Data Warehouse without truncation and will remain available for the observation periods required by CRR Art. 180.

sections.heading: Economic cycle and good and bad years
sections.text: The correlation of the annual default rates (default years 2012–2025) with Dutch macroeconomic indicators published by CBS was analysed to support the window: the correlation is 0.86 with the number of business bankruptcies, 0.74 with the unemployment rate and −0.58 with real GDP growth lagged by one year. Because default rates correlate significantly with these indicators, a documented criterion classifies a year as bad when annual real GDP growth is negative; on this criterion 2012, 2013 and 2020 are bad years, and indicator values in these years were adverse. Over the last 20 years of the GDP series (2006–2025) the reference proportion of bad years is 20% (2009, 2012, 2013 and 2020), while the observation period contains 3 bad years out of 14 (21.4%), so the proportion of bad years is not smaller than the reference proportion. The maximum observed one-year default rate of the internal data, 3.71% for reference date 30 September 2012, is included in the observation period; no year has been excluded. The window thus spans conditions from recession to expansion as well as a period of public support measures, which are relevant to current and foreseeable economic conditions for Dutch SMEs.

sections.heading: Calculation of one-year default rates
sections.text: One-year default rates are calculated quarterly at obligor level with overlapping one-year windows, and the long-run average default rate is the arithmetic average of the 52 quarterly rates, in line with CRM-STD-100 §8.2. The denominator contains all obligors that are not in default at the reference date and have at least one on- or off-balance-sheet credit obligation in the range of application; the numerator contains those obligors with at least one default event during the following 12 months. Obligors whose facilities migrate to another rating system, are repaid, written off or sold during the outcome window remain in the calculation; the bias from obligors leaving the portfolio without a default flag was analysed and is below 0.02 percentage points. Each defaulted obligor is counted only once in the numerator and denominator of a one-year window, even where it defaulted more than once within the window. Observations are removed from the default rates only when the default was wrongly classified (technical past due, numerator only) or the obligor was wrongly assigned to the range of application (numerator and denominator). For grade-level default rates the grade after overrides is used, without substitution effects of credit risk mitigation and without conservative adjustments. Obligors that hold products in both CoreBank SME and the business mortgage system are matched on the Bank-wide party identifier so that every common obligor is counted once.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For reference dates from 1 December 2020, when CR-STD-110 v2.0 fully implemented EBA/GL/2016/07 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171, the RDS default flag equals the production default flag without deviation. For January 2016 to November 2020 the default flag was recalculated in the RDS build from the daily days-past-due counters, materiality components, UTP flags and probation status captured in the source systems since 1 January 2016, applying the current definition; the historical production flag, which used the previous definition, differs from the recalculated flag for 2.9% of default events. For 2012 to 2015 the flag is an approximation from monthly arrears and restructuring data (section 3.3.5); each of the three definitions underlying the calibration data (approximated, recalculated and production) was analysed separately against the current definition. The data window will be extended with each annual review so that the share of data collected under the current definition, now five years (December 2020 to December 2025), increases, and the related MoC is reassessed each time.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: Default is recognised when the obligor is more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation, with materiality thresholds of EUR 100 (absolute) and 1% (relative) for retail exposures, or when the obligor is considered unlikely to pay. The definition is applied as set out in CR-STD-110 v2.0; sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.6 describe the counting of days past due, technical past due and schedule changes, the level of application, probation and multiple defaults, the historical approximation and the reconciliation with the production flag. The default flag in the RDS is constructed in accordance with CR-STD-110, including the materiality thresholds, the UTP triggers of section 3.4, the probation periods and the treatment of multiple defaults. The same definition of default is applied in the IRB approach, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting and credit risk management for this portfolio, and the same RDS default events are used by the SME LGD model (MDL-05) of the same rating system.

sections.heading: Days past due and materiality threshold
sections.text: Days past due are counted daily in CoreBank SME for all obligors, starting on the first day on which both the absolute and the relative component of the materiality threshold are exceeded and restarting from zero when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component of EUR 100 is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component is that sum divided by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure excluding equity exposures, with the level of 1% set by the competent authority. These thresholds are the single thresholds set by the competent authority for retail exposures and apply to all obligors in the range of application; all exposures are denominated in euro, so no currency conversion of the absolute component arises. An obligor is defaulted when both components have been exceeded for more than 90 consecutive days, and the default flag is activated for all exposures of the obligor at the onset of the 91st day; months-in-arrears proxies are not used from 2016 onwards. Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date counts as past due, and once the past-due criterion is met the obligor is classified as defaulted without additional expert judgement. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met and is stored for every default event in the default register and in the RDS. The regulatory thresholds have applied in production since 1 December 2020, and the RDS variable dflag_def_version identifies for each observation whether the flag is approximated, recalculated or taken from production under the regulatory threshold. No internal threshold lower than the regulatory threshold is used, so no separate UTP trigger for lower past-due amounts exists.

sections.heading: Schedule changes, re-ageing and technical past due
sections.text: Where the payment schedule is modified by suspension, deferral or extension, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and where the change is a forbearance measure the distressed restructuring test of section 3.4.1 is performed. Re-ageing of facilities is not permitted: arrears are reset only by payment of the amounts past due or by a restructuring assessed under section 3.4.1, and credit balances on other accounts of the obligor are netted with past-due amounts only where a contractual right of set-off exists and is exercised. Instalments suspended under contractual rights or by law, including the tax and repayment deferrals granted to SMEs in 2020–2021, are not counted as past due, and the reasons for such suspensions were reviewed by Arrears Management for indications of unlikeliness to pay. Technical past due is recognised only for data or system errors of the Bank, payment execution failures and payment allocation time lags, never for wrong credit decisions; each case is documented and corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management. The 311 default observations caused by technical past due were removed from the defaulted observations of the RDS (numerator only).

sections.heading: Level of application, joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: Default is identified at obligor level: the option to apply the definition at facility level for retail exposures is not used, and when an obligor is in default all its credit obligations to the Bank are flagged as defaulted. The obligor-level application reflects internal risk management practice for SMEs, where limits, arrears management and restructuring are managed per client, and it has been applied consistently over the whole observation period. Joint credit obligations of partners in a partnership or of spouses of a sole proprietor are treated in accordance with section 8 of EBA/GL/2016/07: the default of a joint obligation is propagated to the individual exposures of each co-obligor unless Credit Risk Management documents that this is not justified, and a joint obligor is treated as a separate obligor in the materiality threshold calculation. The default of an obligor is identified consistently across CoreBank SME, the business mortgage system and the credit card platform through the central default register, which propagates the status to all systems in the nightly batch. All exposures in scope are booked in a single legal entity in the Netherlands, so the same definition of default is used for all of them and no legal impediments to the exchange of client data arise.

sections.heading: Probation periods, cures and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months in which no default trigger applies and after an assessment by Arrears Management that the improvement of its credit quality, based on its behaviour and financial situation during the probation period, is factual and permanent. After a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring date, the end of any grace period and the date of default, and return to non-default additionally requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule, no amount past due and no remaining concerns about full repayment. The probation start date and probation status are recorded for every default event from 2016 onwards; for 2012–2015 probation periods could not be reconstructed, and cures in that period are taken at the first month-end without arrears above the threshold, which is recorded as part of deficiency DD-01. An obligor defaulting again within 12 months of returning to non-default status is treated as a single default event starting on the first date of default; the RDS links such events through a default episode identifier, and 1,046 events were merged in this way. A subsequent default more than 12 months after cure is treated as a new default event. Of the default events since 2016, 38.4% cured and 9.8% of cured obligors defaulted again within 12 months; Credit Risk Management analyses these re-default rates by trigger annually, and the 2025 analysis concluded that the probation periods are effective and need not be extended.

sections.heading: Reconciliation with the production default flag
sections.text: The default flag constructed by the RDS build code was reconciled with the production default flag of the default register for all reference dates from December 2020, when both are available: 99.94% of obligor-quarter observations agree, and the 41 differing default events are explained by backdated UTP classifications recorded after the monthly extraction. The default flags used for IRB and IFRS 9 purposes are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems; the reconciliation for the four quarters of 2025 showed no unexplained differences for the SME portfolio. The prudential default status and the accounting credit-impaired status are held as two distinctly labelled data elements (dflag_prud and ifrs9_stage3_flag) in the RDS, and their definitional difference, limited to purchased or originated credit-impaired assets not present in this portfolio, is documented in the data dictionary. The definition of default is used for own funds requirements and in internal risk management: the default status drives exposure monitoring, the watch list, arrears management and the monthly credit risk report to senior management. Default identification is automated for all past-due and most UTP triggers, manual UTP assessments follow documented procedures, and the completeness of default identification is controlled by the monthly reconciliation of the default register with arrears and provisioning data.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The UTP triggers are documented in CR-STD-110 §6, mapped to source-system fields and applied consistently to the SME portfolio over the whole period since 2016; the mapping used by the RDS build is listed in Annex A. The following automatic triggers lead to default without further assessment: non-accrued status of a credit obligation; a specific credit risk adjustment resulting from a significant perceived decline in credit quality, including every Stage 3 loss allowance; sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related economic loss above 5%; a distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; bankruptcy or similar protection sought by or filed against the obligor; and the forced sale of collateral or calling of a guarantee by the Bank because of the obligor's inability to pay. Specific credit risk adjustments reflecting a significant perceived decline in credit quality are treated as UTP indications, whereas collective allowances for Stage 1 and Stage 2 exposures are not; every exposure classified as credit-impaired (Stage 3) under IFRS 9 is defaulted, as no exception for exposures below the materiality threshold is applied in this portfolio. The obligor is considered unlikely to pay when the Bank considers it unlikely to pay its obligations in full without recourse to realising security, as assessed through the triggers above and the indicators of section 3.4.1.

sections.heading: Sales, distressed restructuring and case-by-case indicators
sections.text: For every sale of SME credit obligations the reasons for the sale and the loss are analysed by Credit Risk Management; the credit-related economic loss is calculated as L = (E − P)/E, and obligations sold with a loss above 5% are defaulted; the two portfolio sales of 2017 and 2023 concerned only exposures that were already defaulted. For each forbearance measure the diminished financial obligation is calculated as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0, discounting the expected cash flows before and after the restructuring at the original effective interest rate, and exposures above the threshold of 1% are defaulted. Forborne exposures below this threshold are assessed for other indications of unlikeliness to pay, such as a large final instalment, an irregular or back-loaded schedule, a significant grace period or repeated forbearance, and all exposures classified as forborne non-performing are defaulted. The following indicators lead to a case-by-case UTP assessment by the account manager and Arrears Management, completed within 30 days of detection: fraud by the obligor, a significant decline in turnover or cash flow, breach of material covenants, multiple forbearance measures, default of a connected client, default at another institution where known, and loss of a major customer. The identification of these indicators uses external information such as bankruptcy and suspension-of-payment publications in the Central Insolvency Register, Chamber of Commerce updates, bureau payment signals and press reports, in addition to internal early-warning signals. The forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly for indications of unlikeliness to pay, and it is verified monthly that all forborne non-performing exposures are flagged as defaulted.

sections.heading: Operationalisation of default identification
sections.text: For each trigger and indicator the identification method, the internal and external information sources, the responsible unit and the monitoring frequency are documented in the SME default identification procedure (CRM-PRC-114 v3.1), which is referenced in Annex A. Default status is propagated to all IT systems in the nightly batch, and a monthly control compares the default dates in the default register with the dates recorded in the product systems; delays in recording did not cause differences in the RDS because the RDS takes the default date from the default register.

sections.heading: Register of default definitions
sections.text: Credit Risk Management maintains a register of all current and past definitions of default, recording for each version its scope, approving body and date, implementation date, description of changes and, for the IRB approach, the change category and the dates of supervisory notification; the register lists version 1.0 (January 2016, capture of default components) and version 2.0 (December 2020, full implementation of EBA/GL/2016/07 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171). The definition of default and its scope of application were approved by the Management Board on the recommendation of the Group Risk Committee on 24 November 2020. Internal Audit reviewed the robustness, effectiveness and timeliness of the default identification process in audit IA-2025-017 (report of 14 October 2025) and reported its conclusions to the Management Board and the Audit Committee. The implementation of version 2.0 was classified as a material change to all IRB rating systems under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 and was approved by the ECB before it was applied; no change to the definition of default is part of model version 2.0. Risk differentiation under the current definition is demonstrated on reference dates from December 2020 to December 2024 in section 7.1 of the MDD (Gini 0.71 on the out-of-time sample).

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from seven sources: CoreBank SME (accounts, limits, balances and arrears), the business mortgage system (loans and collateral links), the central default register DR-CRM, the customer master data system (party identifiers, legal form, incorporation date and sector code), the financial statements database FSD (annual accounts of legal entities and tax-return based income data of sole proprietors), the Payments Data Hub (monthly aggregates of current account transactions) and the external business credit bureau feed. Each source is extracted by month-end snapshot through the Risk Data Warehouse (RDW), which is the authoritative source for risk data used by the model; extraction reference dates range from 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2025, and all snapshots used for the frozen RDS were taken on 12 June 2026. The lineage from each source system field through the RDW staging and integration layers to each RDS variable, including every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the ETL job or build-code module and the extraction frequency, is documented in Annex A. Lineage is documented for every model variable and for the discarded variables used to construct retained variables, for example daily balances used to derive utilisation and volatility features. The RDS variables are mapped to the data domains Business Banking Credit, Customer, Financial Statements, Payments and Default, each with one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue. The Bank-wide party identifier and the Group naming conventions for legal entities, counterparties and accounts are used throughout, which allows consistent aggregation across source systems. The data governance practices of DATA-POL-001, which implement chapter 3.2 of the ECB Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, apply to all RDS sources.

sections.heading: Manual interventions and lineage changes
sections.text: The only manual intervention in the data flow is the mapping table from the Dutch SBI 2008 activity codes to the eight sector risk groups used by the model; this table is maintained as a version-controlled file (config/sbi_sector_map_v3.csv) in the build repository, subject to four-eyes review and recorded as expert judgement EJ-SME-02. All other steps of the RDS build, including the construction of the default flag and of all features, are performed by build code without manual data manipulation, so that the data are aggregated on a fully automated basis. Two lineage changes occurred in the observation period: the move of current account transaction aggregates from the legacy payments mart to the Payments Data Hub in 2019 and the replacement of the bureau data product in October 2019; both were documented in the lineage before the changed data were used, and their effect on the features was analysed (deficiency DD-03). Changes to the definition, source or transformation of data elements used by the model require approval by the Data Owner and advance notice to the model owner under the data change process of the Group Data Catalogue; no such change occurred between the RDS freeze and the date of this document.

sections.heading: External data
sections.text: Internal data are the only source of the default flag and of the default rates used for calibration; no external or pooled data are used for risk quantification. External data are used only as risk drivers: the bureau payment behaviour index, the number of registered payment disputes and the bureau's legal event flags, delivered monthly by the Bank's contracted business credit bureau under contract TPR-2021-044, and public registration data of the Chamber of Commerce. For each external variable the lineage starts at the point of receipt in the Bank's secure file gateway and records the provider, the data product (Bureau SME Payment Index v4 until September 2019, v5 thereafter) and the delivery date. The bureau provider supplied its methodology documentation, population coverage and the definition of its payment index, which allowed the Bank to assess representativeness: bureau coverage of the Bank's SME obligors is 96.8%, and the index distribution of matched obligors is comparable with the provider's population for the same size classes. Because the bureau data are not used as target or calibration data, differences between the bureau's negative event definitions and the Bank's definition of default do not affect the default flag; the bureau legal event flags were nevertheless compared with the internal default events, and 88% of internal defaults since 2016 were preceded by a bureau event.

sections.heading: Point-in-time feature construction and leakage prevention
sections.text: Every feature is constructed point-in-time from information available at the reference date in production: behavioural features use snapshots up to the reference date, financial statements are used from their registration date in FSD rather than their balance sheet date, and bureau data are taken from the latest delivery before the reference date. Features derived from the target, from post-default processes or from processes triggered by the outcome, such as the transfer to Financial Restructuring and Recovery or collection status, are excluded from the candidate list. No candidate feature has a univariate AUC above 0.90; the leakage review required for features whose removal reduces model AUC by more than five percentage points was performed for max_dpd_12m (reduction 5.4 percentage points) and concluded that the feature uses only arrears history before the reference date. The RDS stores risk driver values at every quarterly reference date, so for defaulted obligors the values over the four quarters before default are available and reflect the monthly update frequency of behavioural data and the annual update of financial statements. Financial statement features use the most recent annual accounts registered at the reference date; for 7.8% of legal-entity observations these accounts are older than 24 months, and the age of the accounts (fin_stmt_age_months) is offered to the model as a feature rather than applying a separate conservative adjustment.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Starting from 5,271,451 raw obligor-quarter observations, four exclusions were applied, each with a documented reason and approved by the model owner on 26 June 2026. EX-01, obligors outside the range of application because the exposure of the group of connected clients exceeded EUR 1 million or the obligor is rated in the corporate rating system: 61,204 observations (1.16%), 3,120 obligors, 1,012 default observations. EX-02, internal, test and staff accounts: 3,418 observations (0.06%), 212 obligors, no default observations. EX-03, duplicate party records created by the 2014 customer master data merge, of which one record per obligor is retained: 12,877 observations (0.24%), 1,588 obligors, 214 default observations. EX-04, facilities without a valid link to a party in 2012–2013: 9,640 observations (0.18%), 2,410 obligors, 187 default observations. In total 87,139 observations (1.65%) and 1,413 default observations were excluded; no exclusion exceeds 5% of records or exposure in any segment, so no additional approval or reporting was required, and the number and share of records excluded by reason is also reported in the data quality report. EX-01 concerns observations wrongly assigned to the model's scope and is removed from numerator and denominator, while EX-02 to EX-04 remove invalid or duplicate records; the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that the exclusions do not affect representativeness or the LRA materially.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing values missing for a structural reason (for example no annual accounts for sole proprietors, no behavioural history for clients with a relationship shorter than six months), values missing at random and values missing because of a data deficiency. Structurally missing values are not imputed; the gradient boosting algorithm learns a default split direction for missing values, and its effect on the explanations is assessed in the explainability report EVD-04-XAI. The only imputation concerns annual turnover of sole proprietors for 2012–2014 (deficiency DD-02): missing values are imputed by the median per SBI sector group and employee size class of 2015, a reproducible method coded in rds_build/impute.py; the imputed share is 11.4% of the 2012–2014 observations of this segment and 2.9% of all observations of the feature, and re-estimation without imputed records changes the out-of-time Gini by less than 0.1 percentage points. Outliers of continuous ratio features are identified as values below the 0.5th or above the 99.5th percentile of the development sample and are capped at these percentiles; the caps are stored in the parameter table feature_caps_v2.0 and applied identically in production, and removing the caps changes the out-of-time Gini by 0.2 percentage points and the portfolio average PD by less than 0.5%. Missing values or outliers in the target variable are not imputed: 38 default events with a missing default date were investigated with Arrears Management and corrected at source in the default register before the RDS freeze.

sections.heading: Sample definition
sections.text: The data were split before any feature selection or hyperparameter tuning into a development sample (reference dates 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2022, 4,318,640 observations) and an out-of-time test sample (reference dates 31 March 2023 to 31 December 2024, 865,672 observations, outcomes up to December 2025), so that the out-of-time portion covers the most recent 12 months of outcomes and more. The development sample was split by obligor into a training part (80%, 3,454,912 observations and 73,244 default observations) and an out-of-sample test part (20%, 863,728 observations and 18,311 default observations); the out-of-time sample contains 12,660 default observations (1.46%). The split by obligor ensures that no obligor appears in both the training and out-of-sample test parts, and the random assignment is reproducible from the stored seed (20260917).

sections.heading: Representativeness of risk drivers
sections.text: Representativeness is tested with the metrics prescribed by CRM-STD-100 §6.5 and MV-HB-003 §6: the PSI per risk driver and on the score for risk differentiation, and two-sample tests of proportions on default rates per segment and grade for risk quantification. The development sample was compared with the application portfolio at 30 June 2026 (108,960 non-defaulted obligors, 146,300 facilities, EAD EUR 6.12 billion) with respect to scope, definition of default, risk characteristics and lending standards; scope and definition of default are identical, and lending standards are analysed in section 5.1.2. The PSI of the model score is 0.06, and the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.14; the only amber value, 0.14 for the bureau payment index, results from the provider's recalibration of its index in 2025 and has no material effect on the grade distribution (grade PSI 0.04). The mix of legal forms (sole proprietors 47%, partnerships 16%, legal entities 37% of obligors), sectors and products in the current portfolio lies within the range observed in the RDS; business credit cards are slightly under-represented in early years but form only 3% of exposure. No material difference in key risk characteristics was found, so no alternative sample or additional risk driver was required. Detailed tables per feature, segment and reference year are provided in Annex B.

sections.heading: Lending standards, recovery policies and seasoning
sections.text: Three significant changes in the observation period were analysed by comparing RDS data before and after each change: the introduction of automated credit acceptance for applications up to EUR 250,000 in 2014, the centralisation of SME collections in 2019 and the tightening of the SME credit policy in 2022 (minimum debt service coverage of 1.2 and stricter treatment of start-ups). After the 2014 change, default rates of newly originated obligors in comparable score bands did not differ significantly; after the 2022 change, the default rate of new obligors in the first two years fell by 18% relative, which is reflected in the Category B margin of conservatism MOC-SME-B2. Expected changes of the default risk over the life of the exposures (seasoning) were analysed on term loans and credit lines: the default rate peaks between 18 and 30 months after origination and declines thereafter, an effect captured by the features relationship length and months since last limit increase. The analysis of lending standards and recovery policies also forms part of the representativeness analysis of section 5.1.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The impact of the exclusions on representativeness was analysed by re-running the representativeness tests and the LRA calculation on the RDS including EX-02 to EX-04 (EX-01 is out of scope by definition): the LRA changes from 2.08% to 2.07%, and the PSI of every model feature between the RDS with and without these exclusions is below 0.01. The aggregate effect of all exclusions on the long-run average default rate is therefore −0.01 percentage points, which is reported to the model owner and was taken into account in the approval of the exclusions. The exclusion of EX-01 moves 3,120 obligors to the corporate rating system, where their defaults are included in that system's RDS.

sections.heading: Sources of bias in the data
sections.text: Four sources of bias were analysed: historical decision bias, because the RDS contains only obligors accepted by the Bank; label bias, because part of the UTP classifications rest on human judgement; under-representation of start-ups and of the agricultural sector; and measurement bias in self-reported turnover of sole proprietors. Decision bias is limited for a behavioural model on existing clients, and the rejection rate of SME applications was stable at 21–24% over the period; label bias is addressed by the labelling analysis of section 3.4.2; under-represented segments were checked separately for discriminatory power (start-ups younger than two years: out-of-time Gini 0.66); and self-reported turnover is replaced by tax-return data where available from 2015. Mitigation by reweighting of start-ups was tested and rejected because it changed the out-of-time Gini by less than 0.1 percentage points and increased the variance of grade PDs. These analyses form part of the data governance of the training, validation and testing data with respect to relevance, representativeness, errors, completeness and bias, as required for high-risk AI systems provided by the Bank.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development against the mandatory dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness and the additional dimensions validity, uniqueness and appropriateness of MRM-STD-022, using 164 DQ rules on 52 critical data elements; the results per rule, variable and dimension are reported in the SME RDS data quality report EVD-04-DQ v1.0 of 19 June 2026. Completeness was measured at record level against the portfolio in the general ledger and at attribute level; accuracy by reconciliation of balances and limits to the general ledger and by a sample-based file review; consistency between RDS and production input data, over time and between related fields; and timeliness as the delay of availability and the currency of financial statements. Validity and uniqueness rules were applied to all CDEs, and appropriateness is addressed by the representativeness analyses of chapter 5. The process for vetting data inputs thus covers accuracy, completeness and appropriateness, and the data used for development and as model inputs are sufficiently precise and free of biases that would distort grade assignment. The assessment concluded that the data are fit for the intended use, and it was signed off by the model developer and the model owner on 19 June 2026 before the RDS was frozen on 26 June 2026.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: Deficiencies were identified and are recorded in the data deficiency log of the model with an identifier, the affected period, variables and segments, the DQ dimension, cause, impact and treatment. DD-01, default flag approximated for 2012–2015 without relative threshold and probation (consistency). DD-02, turnover of sole proprietors missing for 2012–2014 (completeness), imputed as described in section 4.3. DD-03, bureau payment index missing for April–June 2016 and definition change in October 2019. DD-04, collateral values missing for 6.2% of business mortgage observations before 2015. DD-05, orphan facilities 2012–2013, excluded as EX-04. The mapping of the deficiencies to the margin of conservatism categories and to the limitations log of the MDD will be added once the MoC quantification is finalised.

sections.heading: Expert judgement in data treatment
sections.text: Three expert judgements were applied in data treatment and are recorded in the expert judgement log of the model (EJ-SME log v1.4, stored with the model documentation): EJ-SME-01, the approximation rule for the default flag before 2016; EJ-SME-02, the SBI sector mapping table; and EJ-SME-03, the imputation of missing turnover. Each log entry records the type, life cycle stage and affected data, the rationale and the evidence relied on, the alternatives considered and rejected, the quantified impact, the proposer, the approver, the approval date, a review date and the conditions under which the judgement expires. EJ-SME-01 was classified as medium materiality (effect on the LRA 3.4% relative), proposed by S. de Vries, challenged by T. Kuipers, who proposed the alternative with a reconstructed three-month probation that was adopted in the MoC sensitivity analysis, and approved by the model owner and the head of SME Credit Risk Modelling on 2 June 2026. EJ-SME-01 and EJ-SME-03 address data deficiencies DD-01 and DD-02 and are cross-referenced to the data deficiency log and to the Category A MoC components MOC-SME-A1 and MOC-SME-A2. The rationale of each judgement is stated with the underlying data analysis (for example the 2016 overlap comparison for EJ-SME-01), so that a third party can replicate its effect, and the impact of each material judgement was quantified by sensitivity analysis.

sections.heading: Personal data: purpose and lawful basis
sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of self-employed natural persons, partners and directors-owners, who are data subjects under the GDPR; the purposes of processing (development, validation and application of the IRB PD model and its monitoring) are specified in the Record of Processing entry RoP-CR-0147, which is referenced in the model inventory and the AI Inventory. The lawful basis for the IRB use is Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR in conjunction with the CRR requirements to estimate and validate risk parameters, and for internal credit risk management Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, supported by legitimate interest assessment LIA-2026-019, which documents purpose, necessity and the balancing against the interests of data subjects; both were recorded before processing started. The data were collected for the administration of credit agreements and payment accounts, and their use for credit risk measurement is a purpose stated in the Bank's general terms for business clients and in the Record of Processing. Clients are informed in the Bank's privacy statement for business clients that their data are used for credit risk models, so the processing is lawful, fair and transparent. Compliance with these principles is demonstrated by the Record of Processing, the DPIA and the privacy controls in this chapter, which the Privacy Office reviewed on 8 January 2027.

sections.heading: DPIA and data minimisation
sections.text: A DPIA was required because the model scores natural persons for credit decisions, uses ML on personal data and is Tier 1; DPIA-2026-061 was completed on 30 April 2026 before the RDS was built. The DPIA describes the processing and its purposes, assesses necessity and proportionality, assesses the risks to data subjects (in particular discrimination, opacity and incorrect data) and sets out the mitigating measures: pseudonymisation, exclusion of protected attributes, proxy screening, fairness testing, human review of credit decisions and access restrictions. The Data Protection Officer advised on 22 April 2026 that the residual risk is acceptable, so no prior consultation of the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens was required. Every personal data attribute in the RDS is justified by its relevance to the prediction of default in the data dictionary; attributes without predictive relevance, such as names, addresses, dates of birth and nationality, are not extracted, and only the attributes needed for each purpose are made accessible to each role.

sections.heading: Pseudonymisation, security and retention
sections.text: Development and validation use pseudonymised data: party and account identifiers are replaced by keyed tokens (HMAC-SHA-256), and the keys are held by the Data Custodian team of the Chief Data Office, separately from the modelling team. The RDS is held in the approved secure analytics environment MDP-SEC with role-based access for eight named developers and the assigned validators, encryption at rest and logging of all queries. The personal data attributes used are listed in Annex A with their purpose in the model, the lawful basis, the pseudonymisation applied and the retention period. The RDS and development snapshots are retained for the period of use of the model plus five years after decommissioning, which is not longer than necessary for the regulatory purpose. These measures implement data protection by design and data minimisation for the processing of personal data by the model, in line with PRIV-POL-001.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-SME-PD-2026.1 used for the development, calibration and testing of the PD Retail SME model version 2.0 (model identifier MDL-04), the gradient boosting rating system that assigns 12-month PDs to the Bank's retail SME exposures under the A-IRB approach. The range of application comprises retail exposures to self-employed natural persons (sole proprietors), partnerships and legal entities that qualify as SMEs, whose total amount owed by the group of connected clients does not exceed EUR 1 million and which are managed as part of a pool of exposures with similar characteristics, as required for the retail exposure class under CRR Art. 123 and 147(5). Products in scope are business current account credit lines, business term loans, owner-occupied business mortgage loans and business credit cards booked by the Bank's Dutch business banking entity; leasing and factoring exposures are booked in other Group entities and are outside the range of application. The RDS serves three uses: risk differentiation (training and testing of the ranking model), risk quantification (calibration of grade PDs to the long-run average default rate) and the quantification of the margin of conservatism. The document follows the RDS template of Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0; sections added to the template (for example 2.3, 2.4, 3.5 and 5.4) are numbered after the last template section of the relevant chapter so that the template numbering is preserved.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains 52 quarterly reference dates from 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2024, each followed by a 12-month outcome window, so that default outcomes are observed until 31 December 2025. It holds 5,184,312 obligor-quarter observations of 214,580 unique obligors with 402,910 unique facilities, 27,940 default events after the linking of multiple defaults, and 104,215 observations with a default in the 12-month outcome window (2.01%). The unit of observation is the non-defaulted obligor at a reference date; on average 99,700 obligors are observed per reference date, rising from 86,400 in 2012 to 111,900 in 2024. The default proportion of the development sample (2.12%) is higher than the one-year default rate of the application portfolio at reference date 30 June 2025 (1.61%); the difference reflects the inclusion of the 2012–2014 recession years and is documented in section 5.1.1.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts at 31 March 2012, the first quarter-end after the migration of business banking accounts from the legacy system BBS to CoreBank SME in 2011; obligor-level limit, arrears and transaction histories before that date were not migrated and cannot be linked to the current party identifiers. All relevant internal data after the migration are used, so the observation period is a continuous span of 14 default years that includes the five most recent years and extends well beyond them. The window covers the 2012–2013 Dutch recession, with the highest number of business bankruptcies since 1981, the recovery years 2014–2019, the COVID-19 period with government support measures in 2020–2021 and the energy price and inflation shock of 2022–2023, and therefore contains a mix of good and bad years including a downturn. The historical data required for the estimation, including rating histories, default events and exposure histories since 2012, are retained in the Risk Data Warehouse without truncation and will remain available for the observation periods required by CRR Art. 180.

sections.heading: Economic cycle and good and bad years
sections.text: The correlation of the annual default rates (default years 2012–2025) with Dutch macroeconomic indicators published by CBS was analysed to support the window: the correlation is 0.86 with the number of business bankruptcies, 0.74 with the unemployment rate and −0.58 with real GDP growth lagged by one year. Because default rates correlate significantly with these indicators, a documented criterion classifies a year as bad when annual real GDP growth is negative; on this criterion 2012, 2013 and 2020 are bad years, and indicator values in these years were adverse. Over the last 20 years of the GDP series (2006–2025) the reference proportion of bad years is 20% (2009, 2012, 2013 and 2020), while the observation period contains 3 bad years out of 14 (21.4%), so the proportion of bad years is not smaller than the reference proportion. The maximum observed one-year default rate of the internal data, 3.71% for reference date 30 September 2012, is included in the observation period; no year has been excluded. The window thus spans conditions from recession to expansion as well as a period of public support measures, which are relevant to current and foreseeable economic conditions for Dutch SMEs.

sections.heading: Calculation of one-year default rates
sections.text: One-year default rates are calculated quarterly at obligor level with overlapping one-year windows, and the long-run average default rate is the arithmetic average of the 52 quarterly rates, in line with CRM-STD-100 §8.2. The denominator contains all obligors that are not in default at the reference date and have at least one on- or off-balance-sheet credit obligation in the range of application; the numerator contains those obligors with at least one default event during the following 12 months. Obligors whose facilities migrate to another rating system, are repaid, written off or sold during the outcome window remain in the calculation; the bias from obligors leaving the portfolio without a default flag was analysed and is below 0.02 percentage points. Each defaulted obligor is counted only once in the numerator and denominator of a one-year window, even where it defaulted more than once within the window. Observations are removed from the default rates only when the default was wrongly classified (technical past due, numerator only) or the obligor was wrongly assigned to the range of application (numerator and denominator). For grade-level default rates the grade after overrides is used, without substitution effects of credit risk mitigation and without conservative adjustments. Obligors that hold products in both CoreBank SME and the business mortgage system are matched on the Bank-wide party identifier so that every common obligor is counted once.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For reference dates from 1 December 2020, when CR-STD-110 v2.0 fully implemented EBA/GL/2016/07 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171, the RDS default flag equals the production default flag without deviation. For January 2016 to November 2020 the default flag was recalculated in the RDS build from the daily days-past-due counters, materiality components, UTP flags and probation status captured in the source systems since 1 January 2016, applying the current definition; the historical production flag, which used the previous definition, differs from the recalculated flag for 2.9% of default events. For 2012 to 2015 the flag is an approximation from monthly arrears and restructuring data (section 3.3.5); each of the three definitions underlying the calibration data (approximated, recalculated and production) was analysed separately against the current definition. The data window will be extended with each annual review so that the share of data collected under the current definition, now five years (December 2020 to December 2025), increases, and the related MoC is reassessed each time.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: Default is recognised when the obligor is more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation, with materiality thresholds of EUR 100 (absolute) and 1% (relative) for retail exposures, or when the obligor is considered unlikely to pay. The definition is applied as set out in CR-STD-110 v2.0; sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.6 describe the counting of days past due, technical past due and schedule changes, the level of application, probation and multiple defaults, the historical approximation and the reconciliation with the production flag. The default flag in the RDS is constructed in accordance with CR-STD-110, including the materiality thresholds, the UTP triggers of section 3.4, the probation periods and the treatment of multiple defaults. The same definition of default is applied in the IRB approach, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting and credit risk management for this portfolio, and the same RDS default events are used by the SME LGD model (MDL-05) of the same rating system.

sections.heading: Days past due and materiality threshold
sections.text: Days past due are counted daily in CoreBank SME for all obligors, starting on the first day on which both the absolute and the relative component of the materiality threshold are exceeded and restarting from zero when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component of EUR 100 is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component is that sum divided by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure excluding equity exposures, with the level of 1% set by the competent authority. These thresholds are the single thresholds set by the competent authority for retail exposures and apply to all obligors in the range of application; all exposures are denominated in euro, so no currency conversion of the absolute component arises. An obligor is defaulted when both components have been exceeded for more than 90 consecutive days, and the default flag is activated for all exposures of the obligor at the onset of the 91st day; months-in-arrears proxies are not used from 2016 onwards. Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date counts as past due, and once the past-due criterion is met the obligor is classified as defaulted without additional expert judgement. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met and is stored for every default event in the default register and in the RDS. The regulatory thresholds have applied in production since 1 December 2020, and the RDS variable dflag_def_version identifies for each observation whether the flag is approximated, recalculated or taken from production under the regulatory threshold. No internal threshold lower than the regulatory threshold is used, so no separate UTP trigger for lower past-due amounts exists.

sections.heading: Schedule changes, re-ageing and technical past due
sections.text: Where the payment schedule is modified by suspension, deferral or extension, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and where the change is a forbearance measure the distressed restructuring test of section 3.4.1 is performed. Re-ageing of facilities is not permitted: arrears are reset only by payment of the amounts past due or by a restructuring assessed under section 3.4.1, and credit balances on other accounts of the obligor are netted with past-due amounts only where a contractual right of set-off exists and is exercised. Instalments suspended under contractual rights or by law, including the tax and repayment deferrals granted to SMEs in 2020–2021, are not counted as past due, and the reasons for such suspensions were reviewed by Arrears Management for indications of unlikeliness to pay. Technical past due is recognised only for data or system errors of the Bank, payment execution failures and payment allocation time lags, never for wrong credit decisions; each case is documented and corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management. The 311 default observations caused by technical past due were removed from the defaulted observations of the RDS (numerator only).

sections.heading: Level of application, joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: Default is identified at obligor level: the option to apply the definition at facility level for retail exposures is not used, and when an obligor is in default all its credit obligations to the Bank are flagged as defaulted. The obligor-level application reflects internal risk management practice for SMEs, where limits, arrears management and restructuring are managed per client, and it has been applied consistently over the whole observation period. Joint credit obligations of partners in a partnership or of spouses of a sole proprietor are treated in accordance with section 8 of EBA/GL/2016/07: the default of a joint obligation is propagated to the individual exposures of each co-obligor unless Credit Risk Management documents that this is not justified, and a joint obligor is treated as a separate obligor in the materiality threshold calculation. The default of an obligor is identified consistently across CoreBank SME, the business mortgage system and the credit card platform through the central default register, which propagates the status to all systems in the nightly batch. All exposures in scope are booked in a single legal entity in the Netherlands, so the same definition of default is used for all of them and no legal impediments to the exchange of client data arise.

sections.heading: Probation periods, cures and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months in which no default trigger applies and after an assessment by Arrears Management that the improvement of its credit quality, based on its behaviour and financial situation during the probation period, is factual and permanent. After a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring date, the end of any grace period and the date of default, and return to non-default additionally requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule, no amount past due and no remaining concerns about full repayment. The probation start date and probation status are recorded for every default event from 2016 onwards; for 2012–2015 probation periods could not be reconstructed, and cures in that period are taken at the first month-end without arrears above the threshold, which is recorded as part of deficiency DD-01. An obligor defaulting again within 12 months of returning to non-default status is treated as a single default event starting on the first date of default; the RDS links such events through a default episode identifier, and 1,046 events were merged in this way. A subsequent default more than 12 months after cure is treated as a new default event. Of the default events since 2016, 38.4% cured and 9.8% of cured obligors defaulted again within 12 months; Credit Risk Management analyses these re-default rates by trigger annually, and the 2025 analysis concluded that the probation periods are effective and need not be extended.

sections.heading: Historical approximation of the default flag (2012–2015)
sections.text: Before 1 January 2016 the components of the current definition were not captured in the source systems, and the default flag is approximated as: arrears of more than 90 days on an obligor-level amount above EUR 100 at a month-end, a transfer to the Financial Restructuring and Recovery department, a bankruptcy registration or a specific provision booked in the loan loss system. The relative materiality component could not be applied because obligor-level on-balance exposure was not stored at a daily frequency, and probation periods could not be reconstructed (section 3.3.4). The effect of the approximation was quantified on the overlap year 2016, in which both the approximation and the recalculated flag are available: the approximation identifies 3.2% fewer defaulted obligors and yields a one-year default rate 0.07 percentage points lower than the recalculated flag, with the difference concentrated in UTP-driven defaults without arrears. The resulting deficiency is recorded as DD-01 in section 6.2 and linked to the Category A margin of conservatism component MOC-SME-A1 in chapter 6 of the MDD, which is based on a sensitivity analysis over alternative approximations.

sections.heading: Reconciliation with the production default flag
sections.text: The default flag constructed by the RDS build code was reconciled with the production default flag of the default register for all reference dates from December 2020, when both are available: 99.94% of obligor-quarter observations agree, and the 41 differing default events are explained by backdated UTP classifications recorded after the monthly extraction. The default flags used for IRB and IFRS 9 purposes are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems; the reconciliation for the four quarters of 2025 showed no unexplained differences for the SME portfolio. The prudential default status and the accounting credit-impaired status are held as two distinctly labelled data elements (dflag_prud and ifrs9_stage3_flag) in the RDS, and their definitional difference, limited to purchased or originated credit-impaired assets not present in this portfolio, is documented in the data dictionary. The definition of default is used for own funds requirements and in internal risk management: the default status drives exposure monitoring, the watch list, arrears management and the monthly credit risk report to senior management. Default identification is automated for all past-due and most UTP triggers, manual UTP assessments follow documented procedures, and the completeness of default identification is controlled by the monthly reconciliation of the default register with arrears and provisioning data.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The UTP triggers are documented in CR-STD-110 §6, mapped to source-system fields and applied consistently to the SME portfolio over the whole period since 2016; the mapping used by the RDS build is listed in Annex A. The following automatic triggers lead to default without further assessment: non-accrued status of a credit obligation; a specific credit risk adjustment resulting from a significant perceived decline in credit quality, including every Stage 3 loss allowance; sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related economic loss above 5%; a distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; bankruptcy or similar protection sought by or filed against the obligor; and the forced sale of collateral or calling of a guarantee by the Bank because of the obligor's inability to pay. Specific credit risk adjustments reflecting a significant perceived decline in credit quality are treated as UTP indications, whereas collective allowances for Stage 1 and Stage 2 exposures are not; every exposure classified as credit-impaired (Stage 3) under IFRS 9 is defaulted, as no exception for exposures below the materiality threshold is applied in this portfolio. The obligor is considered unlikely to pay when the Bank considers it unlikely to pay its obligations in full without recourse to realising security, as assessed through the triggers above and the indicators of section 3.4.1.

sections.heading: Sales, distressed restructuring and case-by-case indicators
sections.text: For every sale of SME credit obligations the reasons for the sale and the loss are analysed by Credit Risk Management; the credit-related economic loss is calculated as L = (E − P)/E, and obligations sold with a loss above 5% are defaulted; the two portfolio sales of 2017 and 2023 concerned only exposures that were already defaulted. For each forbearance measure the diminished financial obligation is calculated as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0, discounting the expected cash flows before and after the restructuring at the original effective interest rate, and exposures above the threshold of 1% are defaulted. Forborne exposures below this threshold are assessed for other indications of unlikeliness to pay, such as a large final instalment, an irregular or back-loaded schedule, a significant grace period or repeated forbearance, and all exposures classified as forborne non-performing are defaulted. The following indicators lead to a case-by-case UTP assessment by the account manager and Arrears Management, completed within 30 days of detection: fraud by the obligor, a significant decline in turnover or cash flow, breach of material covenants, multiple forbearance measures, default of a connected client, default at another institution where known, and loss of a major customer. The identification of these indicators uses external information such as bankruptcy and suspension-of-payment publications in the Central Insolvency Register, Chamber of Commerce updates, bureau payment signals and press reports, in addition to internal early-warning signals. The forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly for indications of unlikeliness to pay, and it is verified monthly that all forborne non-performing exposures are flagged as defaulted.

sections.heading: Operationalisation of default identification
sections.text: For each trigger and indicator the identification method, the internal and external information sources, the responsible unit and the monitoring frequency are documented in the SME default identification procedure (CRM-PRC-114 v3.1), which is referenced in Annex A. Default status is propagated to all IT systems in the nightly batch, and a monthly control compares the default dates in the default register with the dates recorded in the product systems; delays in recording did not cause differences in the RDS because the RDS takes the default date from the default register.

sections.heading: Register of default definitions
sections.text: Credit Risk Management maintains a register of all current and past definitions of default, recording for each version its scope, approving body and date, implementation date, description of changes and, for the IRB approach, the change category and the dates of supervisory notification; the register lists version 1.0 (January 2016, capture of default components) and version 2.0 (December 2020, full implementation of EBA/GL/2016/07 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171). The definition of default and its scope of application were approved by the Management Board on the recommendation of the Group Risk Committee on 24 November 2020. Internal Audit reviewed the robustness, effectiveness and timeliness of the default identification process in audit IA-2025-017 (report of 14 October 2025) and reported its conclusions to the Management Board and the Audit Committee. The implementation of version 2.0 was classified as a material change to all IRB rating systems under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 and was approved by the ECB before it was applied; no change to the definition of default is part of model version 2.0. Risk differentiation under the current definition is demonstrated on reference dates from December 2020 to December 2024 in section 7.1 of the MDD (Gini 0.71 on the out-of-time sample).

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from seven sources: CoreBank SME (accounts, limits, balances and arrears), the business mortgage system (loans and collateral links), the central default register DR-CRM, the customer master data system (party identifiers, legal form, incorporation date and sector code), the financial statements database FSD (annual accounts of legal entities and tax-return based income data of sole proprietors), the Payments Data Hub (monthly aggregates of current account transactions) and the external business credit bureau feed. Each source is extracted by month-end snapshot through the Risk Data Warehouse (RDW), which is the authoritative source for risk data used by the model; extraction reference dates range from 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2025, and all snapshots used for the frozen RDS were taken on 12 June 2026. The lineage from each source system field through the RDW staging and integration layers to each RDS variable, including every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the ETL job or build-code module and the extraction frequency, is documented in Annex A. Lineage is documented for every model variable and for the discarded variables used to construct retained variables, for example daily balances used to derive utilisation and volatility features. The RDS variables are mapped to the data domains Business Banking Credit, Customer, Financial Statements, Payments and Default, each with one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue. The Bank-wide party identifier and the Group naming conventions for legal entities, counterparties and accounts are used throughout, which allows consistent aggregation across source systems. The data governance practices of DATA-POL-001, which implement chapter 3.2 of the ECB Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, apply to all RDS sources.

sections.heading: Manual interventions and lineage changes
sections.text: The only manual intervention in the data flow is the mapping table from the Dutch SBI 2008 activity codes to the eight sector risk groups used by the model; this table is maintained as a version-controlled file (config/sbi_sector_map_v3.csv) in the build repository, subject to four-eyes review and recorded as expert judgement EJ-SME-02. All other steps of the RDS build, including the construction of the default flag and of all features, are performed by build code without manual data manipulation, so that the data are aggregated on a fully automated basis. Two lineage changes occurred in the observation period: the move of current account transaction aggregates from the legacy payments mart to the Payments Data Hub in 2019 and the replacement of the bureau data product in October 2019; both were documented in the lineage before the changed data were used, and their effect on the features was analysed (deficiency DD-03). Changes to the definition, source or transformation of data elements used by the model require approval by the Data Owner and advance notice to the model owner under the data change process of the Group Data Catalogue; no such change occurred between the RDS freeze and the date of this document.

sections.heading: External data
sections.text: Internal data are the only source of the default flag and of the default rates used for calibration; no external or pooled data are used for risk quantification. External data are used only as risk drivers: the bureau payment behaviour index, the number of registered payment disputes and the bureau's legal event flags, delivered monthly by the Bank's contracted business credit bureau under contract TPR-2021-044, and public registration data of the Chamber of Commerce. For each external variable the lineage starts at the point of receipt in the Bank's secure file gateway and records the provider, the data product (Bureau SME Payment Index v4 until September 2019, v5 thereafter) and the delivery date. The bureau provider supplied its methodology documentation, population coverage and the definition of its payment index, which allowed the Bank to assess representativeness: bureau coverage of the Bank's SME obligors is 96.8%, and the index distribution of matched obligors is comparable with the provider's population for the same size classes. Because the bureau data are not used as target or calibration data, differences between the bureau's negative event definitions and the Bank's definition of default do not affect the default flag; the bureau legal event flags were nevertheless compared with the internal default events, and 88% of internal defaults since 2016 were preceded by a bureau event.

sections.heading: Point-in-time feature construction and leakage prevention
sections.text: Every feature is constructed point-in-time from information available at the reference date in production: behavioural features use snapshots up to the reference date, financial statements are used from their registration date in FSD rather than their balance sheet date, and bureau data are taken from the latest delivery before the reference date. Features derived from the target, from post-default processes or from processes triggered by the outcome, such as the transfer to Financial Restructuring and Recovery or collection status, are excluded from the candidate list. No candidate feature has a univariate AUC above 0.90; the leakage review required for features whose removal reduces model AUC by more than five percentage points was performed for max_dpd_12m (reduction 5.4 percentage points) and concluded that the feature uses only arrears history before the reference date. The RDS stores risk driver values at every quarterly reference date, so for defaulted obligors the values over the four quarters before default are available and reflect the monthly update frequency of behavioural data and the annual update of financial statements. Financial statement features use the most recent annual accounts registered at the reference date; for 7.8% of legal-entity observations these accounts are older than 24 months, and the age of the accounts (fin_stmt_age_months) is offered to the model as a feature rather than applying a separate conservative adjustment.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Starting from 5,271,451 raw obligor-quarter observations, four exclusions were applied, each with a documented reason and approved by the model owner on 26 June 2026. EX-01, obligors outside the range of application because the exposure of the group of connected clients exceeded EUR 1 million or the obligor is rated in the corporate rating system: 61,204 observations (1.16%), 3,120 obligors, 1,012 default observations. EX-02, internal, test and staff accounts: 3,418 observations (0.06%), 212 obligors, no default observations. EX-03, duplicate party records created by the 2014 customer master data merge, of which one record per obligor is retained: 12,877 observations (0.24%), 1,588 obligors, 214 default observations. EX-04, facilities without a valid link to a party in 2012–2013: 9,640 observations (0.18%), 2,410 obligors, 187 default observations. In total 87,139 observations (1.65%) and 1,413 default observations were excluded; no exclusion exceeds 5% of records or exposure in any segment, so no additional approval or reporting was required, and the number and share of records excluded by reason is also reported in the data quality report. EX-01 concerns observations wrongly assigned to the model's scope and is removed from numerator and denominator, while EX-02 to EX-04 remove invalid or duplicate records; the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that the exclusions do not affect representativeness or the LRA materially.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing values missing for a structural reason (for example no annual accounts for sole proprietors, no behavioural history for clients with a relationship shorter than six months), values missing at random and values missing because of a data deficiency. Structurally missing values are not imputed; the gradient boosting algorithm learns a default split direction for missing values, and its effect on the explanations is assessed in the explainability report EVD-04-XAI. The only imputation concerns annual turnover of sole proprietors for 2012–2014 (deficiency DD-02): missing values are imputed by the median per SBI sector group and employee size class of 2015, a reproducible method coded in rds_build/impute.py; the imputed share is 11.4% of the 2012–2014 observations of this segment and 2.9% of all observations of the feature, and re-estimation without imputed records changes the out-of-time Gini by less than 0.1 percentage points. Outliers of continuous ratio features are identified as values below the 0.5th or above the 99.5th percentile of the development sample and are capped at these percentiles; the caps are stored in the parameter table feature_caps_v2.0 and applied identically in production, and removing the caps changes the out-of-time Gini by 0.2 percentage points and the portfolio average PD by less than 0.5%. Missing values or outliers in the target variable are not imputed: 38 default events with a missing default date were investigated with Arrears Management and corrected at source in the default register before the RDS freeze.

sections.heading: Sample definition
sections.text: The data were split before any feature selection or hyperparameter tuning into a development sample (reference dates 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2022, 4,318,640 observations) and an out-of-time test sample (reference dates 31 March 2023 to 31 December 2024, 865,672 observations, outcomes up to December 2025), so that the out-of-time portion covers the most recent 12 months of outcomes and more. The development sample was split by obligor into a training part (80%, 3,454,912 observations and 73,244 default observations) and an out-of-sample test part (20%, 863,728 observations and 18,311 default observations); the out-of-time sample contains 12,660 default observations (1.46%). The split by obligor ensures that no obligor appears in both the training and out-of-sample test parts, and the random assignment is reproducible from the stored seed (20260917).

sections.heading: Representativeness of risk drivers
sections.text: Representativeness is tested with the metrics prescribed by CRM-STD-100 §6.5 and MV-HB-003 §6: the PSI per risk driver and on the score for risk differentiation, and two-sample tests of proportions on default rates per segment and grade for risk quantification. The development sample was compared with the application portfolio at 30 June 2026 (108,960 non-defaulted obligors, 146,300 facilities, EAD EUR 6.12 billion) with respect to scope, definition of default, risk characteristics and lending standards; scope and definition of default are identical, and lending standards are analysed in section 5.1.2. The PSI of the model score is 0.06, and the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.14; the only amber value, 0.14 for the bureau payment index, results from the provider's recalibration of its index in 2025 and has no material effect on the grade distribution (grade PSI 0.04). The mix of legal forms (sole proprietors 47%, partnerships 16%, legal entities 37% of obligors), sectors and products in the current portfolio lies within the range observed in the RDS; business credit cards are slightly under-represented in early years but form only 3% of exposure. No material difference in key risk characteristics was found, so no alternative sample or additional risk driver was required. Detailed tables per feature, segment and reference year are provided in Annex B.
