sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The model is developed on the frozen reference data set RDS-SME-PD-2026.1, documented in the SME RDS documentation EVD-04-RDS v1.0 approved on 19 February 2027, with 5,184,312 obligor-quarter observations for the reference dates 31 March 2012 to 31 December 2024. Development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples were defined before estimation: training sample (80% of obligors, reference dates 2012–2022, 3,454,912 observations, default rate 2.12%), out-of-sample test sample (20% of obligors, same dates, 863,728 observations) and out-of-time sample (reference dates 2023–2024, 865,672 observations, default rate 1.46%); the out-of-time sample was not used for feature selection, hyperparameter tuning or parameter estimation. The calibration sample of each calibration segment consists of all 52 reference dates of the RDS for that segment (CS1 2,903,215 observations, CS2 2,281,097 observations); it is stored with the frozen RDS and described in section 5.1. All results in this MDD were produced from the estimation code tag and the RDS version recorded in section 12.2. The PD estimates are derived from the Bank's own historical default experience over 14 default years and all relevant internal data and methods, and not from judgemental considerations alone; expert judgement is limited to the documented adjustments of chapter 11.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data requirements, discriminatory power, stability, interpretability and implementation constraints): a re-estimated logistic regression with weight-of-evidence binning (the version 1.3 approach), a generalised additive model with spline terms and a monotonically constrained gradient boosting classifier. On the out-of-time sample the Gini coefficients were 0.664 for the logistic regression, 0.683 for the additive model and 0.709 for gradient boosting, while the stability over quarterly cohorts was comparable (standard deviation of quarterly Gini 1.1, 1.0 and 0.9 percentage points). The use of the ML technique is justified by a Gini uplift of 4.5 percentage points over the interpretable benchmark, mainly from non-linear interactions between utilisation, transaction inflows and arrears that the linear score cannot capture; the additional risks introduced (opacity, overfitting, instability and bias) are addressed by monotonic constraints, SHAP explanations and reason codes, seed-stability tests, fairness testing and enhanced monitoring. Complexity was limited deliberately: tree depth is capped at four, the feature set is restricted to 27 interpretable features and a deeper configuration with 45 features, which added only 0.4 percentage points of Gini, was rejected. The design is conceptually sound and consistent with the business rationale: the main drivers are the payment and liquidity signals that SME Credit Risk Management uses in its early-warning process.

sections.heading: Long list of candidate risk drivers, expected direction and climate-related drivers
sections.text: The long list of 212 candidate risk drivers combined a statistical screening of all available variables with expert input from SME Credit Risk Management and Arrears Management in two workshops (September 2025), and covers arrears and payment behaviour, account and limit usage, transaction flows, financial statements, bureau information, business characteristics, collateral and relationship data. Before estimation the expected direction of effect was recorded for each candidate with an established risk logic (for example increasing risk with days past due, utilisation and returned direct debits, decreasing risk with turnover, equity ratio and business age); the final model confirms the expected direction for all constrained features. Each candidate was assessed for economic rationale, availability at the point of use in the monthly production run and stability over time (PSI across years below 0.25 and stable univariate Gini sign). The selection of drivers is thus supported by statistical analysis of predictive power and by expert analysis of relevance, and the rationale for the choice of rating criteria is documented per feature in Annex A of the RDS documentation and the Feature Register. The materiality of climate-related and environmental risks for the model was assessed in development: transition risk through the share of exposure to energy-intensive sectors (6.8% of EAD) and physical risk through flood-zone location of business mortgage collateral (2.1% of EAD). Adding an energy-intensity indicator per SBI sector and a flood-zone flag as candidate features did not improve the out-of-time Gini (below 0.1 percentage points) and their SHAP contributions were below the 1% threshold, so these drivers are not material and are not included; the sector risk group captures the sector-level risk. The assessment will be repeated in each annual review and whenever the Bank's climate risk materiality assessment changes.

sections.heading: Feature selection
sections.text: Feature selection was performed on the training sample only: univariate screening (Gini above 0.05, missing share below 70%, PSI across years below 0.25) reduced the long list to 58 features; correlated features (absolute Spearman correlation above 0.8) were resolved by keeping the feature with the higher univariate Gini and clearer interpretation; and a recursive SHAP-based elimination within cross-validation led to the final 27 features. Features with a mean absolute SHAP value below 1% of the total were removed, except the collateral coverage ratio (0.8%), which is retained for a documented business reason, namely its role in the credit acceptance dialogue for business mortgages. All engineered features have an economic or behavioural interpretation, such as the trend in monthly credit turnover or the number of months with an overdraft excess; automatically generated features are not used. Every final feature has a direction and magnitude of effect consistent with economic intuition, as shown by the SHAP dependence analysis in section 7.7, so the estimates are plausible, intuitive and based on the material drivers of default. The input variables thus form a reasonable and effective basis for the predictions.

sections.heading: Algorithm and hyperparameter tuning
sections.text: The classifier is LightGBM 4.3.0 with a binary log-loss objective; each tree splits the feature space into leaves, the final log-odds score is the sum of the leaf values of all trees, and the model is fitted by gradient boosting with shrinkage, as described mathematically in Annex 4.A together with the underlying assumptions. The hyperparameter search covered learning rate (0.01–0.1), number of leaves (7–31), maximum depth (3–6), minimum observations per leaf (200–2,000), feature and bagging fractions (0.6–1.0) and L2 regularisation (0–20); the search used Bayesian optimisation (Optuna TPE, 150 trials) with five-fold cross-validation grouped by obligor and blocked by time within the training sample, the objective being the mean validation AUC penalised by the train–validation gap above three percentage points. The selected hyperparameters are: learning rate 0.03, number of leaves 15, maximum depth 4, minimum 800 observations per leaf, feature fraction 0.8, bagging fraction 0.8 with bagging frequency 1, L2 regularisation 5.0 and 640 trees determined by early stopping after 50 rounds without improvement. The random seed 20260917 is fixed for sampling, bagging and cross-validation folds, and the ordering of training observations (by reference date and pseudonymised obligor token) is fixed in the training script, so that the training can be replicated exactly. The test samples were not used for any tuning decision.

sections.heading: Overfitting controls and monotonic constraints
sections.text: Overfitting is controlled by shrinkage (learning rate 0.03), the depth and leaf limits, the minimum of 800 observations per leaf, L2 regularisation, row and feature subsampling, and early stopping on the grouped cross-validation folds. The Gini gap between the training sample (0.741) and the out-of-sample test sample (0.724) is 1.7 percentage points and between training and the out-of-time sample (0.709) 3.2 percentage points, both below the five-point justification threshold. Monotonic constraints are imposed in the algorithm for the 19 features whose direction is established by the risk logic: increasing (+1) for max_dpd_12m, overdraft_excess_months_6m, util_ratio_avg_6m, returned_debits_6m, balance_volatility_12m, bureau_dispute_count_12m, forbearance_flag_24m, prior_default_60m, limit_increase_request_6m and loan_to_turnover, and decreasing (−1) for bureau_payment_index, inflow_trend_12m, turnover_log, equity_ratio, business_age_years, rel_length_months, min_balance_3m_rel, collateral_coverage and dscr_last_fy. The remaining eight features (sector risk group, legal form, product mix, region-independent seasonality index, fin_stmt_age_months, months since last limit increase, number of accounts and card usage share) have no established direction and are left unconstrained, a choice recorded as expert judgement EJ-SME-04. Compliance with the constraints and the plausibility of the learned relationships were verified with partial dependence and ICE plots on the out-of-time sample in the explainability report EVD-04-XAI.

sections.heading: Calibration target and long-run average default rate
sections.text: Grade PDs are calibrated per calibration segment to the long-run average of one-year default rates, calculated as the arithmetic average of the 52 quarterly overlapping one-year default rates of the RDS: 2.33% for CS1, 1.79% for CS2 and 2.08% for the portfolio before adjustment. The historical observation period (default years 2012–2025) was assessed for a representative mix of good and bad years using default rate variability, macroeconomic indicators and changes in the environment (RDS section 2.3), and contains three bad years in 14 against a reference proportion of 20%. Default rates in 2020–2021 were depressed by government support measures (tax deferral, NOW and TOZO schemes), which delayed defaults rather than preventing them; the appropriate adjustment AA-01 replaces the default rates of reference dates Q2 2020 to Q4 2021 by counterfactual rates from the satellite model of MDL-10 using the observed macro variables, which raises the LRA to 2.41% for CS1, 1.85% for CS2 and 2.16% for the portfolio (EJ-SME-06). No adjustment lowers the LRA below the observed average: the adjusted LRA exceeds both the average of the most recent five years (1.52%) and the all-data average (2.08%). A reference LRA for 2008–2018 cannot be computed because internal data start in 2012; the LRA of the available sub-period 2012–2018 (2.61%) is higher than the adjusted LRA, and the difference is attributed to the 2014 and 2022 changes in credit policy and the inclusion of the benign years 2019–2025.

sections.heading: Calibration method
sections.text: The raw log-odds score s is mapped to a best-estimate PD per calibration segment k with PD = 1/(1 + exp(−(a_k + b_k·s))): the slope b_k is estimated by logistic regression on the training sample (b_CS1 = 0.94, b_CS2 = 0.97), and the intercept a_k is then set so that the average PD over the calibration sample equals the adjusted LRA of the segment. Calibration is performed on the score after taking overrides into account in the realised default rates per grade, and before the application of the MoC and the regulatory PD floor. Because the calibration function is strictly increasing in the score, it does not change the rank ordering of obligors within a calibration segment. Final PDs are pool PDs, not continuous PDs: the pool PD is the average best-estimate PD of the calibration sample observations in the pool, and neither continuous PDs nor smoothing of default rates are used to compensate for lack of data or low discriminatory power or to reduce own funds requirements. For each of the 52 LRA calculation dates the average PD before MoC of each calibration segment is compared with the one-year default rate and with the LRA; these calibration tests are reported in section 7.2.

sections.heading: Grade assignment and master scale
sections.text: Obligors are assigned to pools by comparing their best-estimate PD with the boundaries of the retail master scale of CRM-STD-100 §5.2 (twelve non-defaulted grades R01–R12 and default grade RD), so each pool maps to exactly one master scale grade. The portfolio pool PDs before MoC are R01 0.06%, R02 0.15%, R03 0.27%, R04 0.47%, R05 0.79%, R06 1.35%, R07 2.31%, R08 4.10%, R09 7.40%, R10 13.60%, R11 25.90% and R12 47.50%, increasing monotonically with the grade. No grade contains more than 30% of the exposures: the largest share is 17.3% of EAD in R05, the Herfindahl index of the grade distribution is 0.12, and every pool contains at least 2,100 obligors at the current reference date and at least 30 default observations in the calibration sample (the minimum, 34, in pool R01 of CS2), which is sufficient for meaningful quantification and validation. The calibration was complemented by qualitative analyses of the shape of the obligor distribution, the minimum number of obligors per grade and the avoidance of concentrations. The assignment groups sufficiently homogeneous exposures and differentiates risk meaningfully, as tested in section 7.3.

sections.heading: Final PD and regulatory floor
sections.text: The final PD of each pool is the calibrated best estimate multiplied by (1 + total relative MoC of the calibration segment), with the MoC applied before the regulatory floor. The PD applied to each exposure is at least 0.05% in accordance with CRR Art. 160(1) and 163(1) and CRM-STD-100 §11.1; the PD floor is applied at exposure level after the MoC. At 30 June 2026 the floor is binding for pool R01 of CS2 only, affecting 1,120 obligors (1.0% of obligors) and EUR 58 million of EAD (0.9%). After MoC the pool PDs remain within their master scale grades and increase monotonically with the grade in both calibration segments, so the application of the MoC preserves the rank ordering.

sections.heading: Deficiency identification and appropriate adjustments
sections.text: Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of Annex 1 of CRM-STD-101, covering the RDS, the default definition, the estimation methods and changes in processes and environment; the assessment, including deficiencies considered and rejected, is documented in this chapter. For each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first: AA-01 corrects the depressed default rates of 2020–2021 and the imputation of turnover corrects DD-02, whereas the approximated default flag (DD-01) and the bureau index discontinuity (DD-03) cannot be corrected with sufficient accuracy. The evidence that the adjusted parameter is a best estimate is the back-cast of AA-01 on the pre-2020 years, where the satellite model reproduces the observed default rates with a mean absolute error of 0.09 percentage points. The remaining uncertainty of the appropriate adjustments is included in Category A (DD-02) and Category B (AA-01) MoC, and the MoC is not used to compensate for deficiencies that can be corrected by an appropriate adjustment. Considered and rejected: DD-04 (missing historical collateral values, no effect on the LRA) and the under-representation of business credit cards (3% of EAD, default rate not significantly different). The final estimate consists of the best estimate including appropriate adjustments plus the margin of conservatism, distinguished into Category A (data and methodological deficiencies), Category B (relevant changes) and Category C (general estimation error).

sections.heading: Category A margin of conservatism
sections.text: MOC-SME-A1 (DD-01, approximated default flag 2012–2015): the LRA was re-estimated under three plausible alternative approximations, namely with a relative threshold proxied by the month-end balance, with a reconstructed three-month probation period, and with a 60-day instead of 90-day arrears criterion for obligors in special management; the adverse effects on the LRA ranged from +1.9% to +4.0% for CS1 and +1.7% to +3.6% for CS2, and the MoC is set at the upper end of the range, +4.0% (CS1) and +3.6% (CS2). MOC-SME-A2 (DD-02, imputed turnover of sole proprietors): re-estimation with imputation by the 25th and 75th percentile instead of the median gives adverse effects of +1.1% (CS1) and +0.4% (CS2), which are applied. MOC-SME-A3 (DD-03, bureau index gap and definition change): re-estimation excluding the affected quarters and with an alternative mapping gives +0.6% for both segments. Each deficiency is recorded in the MoC register with a unique identifier, the affected parameter and segments and a reference to the data deficiency log, and is quantified individually per calibration segment before aggregation. No external data with a different default definition are used, so no MoC for external default definitions arises; the deficiencies of the calibration data do not create a representativeness bias beyond what is covered by these components.

sections.heading: Category B margin of conservatism
sections.text: MOC-SME-B1 (government support measures 2020–2021 and the resulting appropriate adjustment AA-01): the LRA was re-estimated with alternative counterfactuals (satellite model with and without the bankruptcy series, and a default-deferral assumption of 12 instead of 18 months); the adverse effects of +2.2% (CS1) and +2.5% (CS2) are applied. MOC-SME-B2 (tightening of the SME credit policy in 2022): because the lower default rate of recent vintages may not persist, the LRA was re-estimated with and without a vintage weighting; the adverse effect of +0.8% for both segments is applied. Both components cover changes to underwriting standards and the economic environment that reduce the representativeness of historical data, and each is quantified per calibration segment.

Both components cover changes to underwriting standards and the economic environment that reduce the representativeness of historical data, and each is quantified per calibration segment.

sections.heading: Category C margin of conservatism
sections.text: The Category C MoC reflects the general estimation error of the LRA: the distribution of the LRA estimator per calibration segment was obtained by a moving-block bootstrap of the 52 quarterly one-year default rates (block length eight quarters, 5,000 replications), which preserves the autocorrelation of the default rate series and widens with fewer observations and shorter time series. The upper bound of the one-sided 90% interval exceeds the LRA by 0.21 percentage points for CS1 and 0.17 percentage points for CS2, giving a Category C MoC of +8.7% and +9.2% respectively. The Category C MoC is therefore greater than zero, and the Category A and B components are non-negative and proportionate to the uncertainty they cover.

sections.heading: Total MoC, register and remediation
sections.text: The total MoC per calibration segment is the simple sum of the Category A, B and C components without diversification: CS1 4.0% + 1.1% + 0.6% + 2.2% + 0.8% + 8.7% = 17.4% and CS2 3.6% + 0.4% + 0.6% + 2.5% + 0.8% + 9.2% = 17.1%, added to the best estimate. The MoC is quantified per category and calibration segment, reflects estimation uncertainty at the level of the final pool estimates, and is larger where data are less satisfactory, as shown by the larger Category A MoC of CS1. The final PDs average 2.83% for CS1 and 2.17% for CS2; the MoC increases the RWEA of the range of application by EUR 196 million, of which EUR 78 million from Category A, EUR 38 million from Category B and EUR 80 million from Category C. The MoC register MOC-REG-MDL04 records per deficiency the category, quantification method, MoC value, calibration segments and remediation status, lists the affected components, and is the complete list of deficiencies required in the model documentation. Each Category A deficiency has a remediation plan with owner and target date or is documented as permanent (DD-01, reassessed annually), and MoC levels are monitored in the annual review, with internal reporting per Category A, B and C to the MRC through the quarterly MoC report of Model Risk Management. The total MoC is below 20% of the best estimate for both segments, so no redevelopment assessment by the MRC is required; any reduction of a component requires confirmation of the remediation by Model Validation, and changes in the MoC are classified under MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power was measured by AUC and Gini on all samples: Gini 0.741 (training), 0.724 (out-of-sample test) and 0.709 (out-of-time, AUC 0.854, 95% DeLong interval for the Gini 0.700–0.718), above the retail threshold of 0.50 of MV-HB-003 and MRM-STD-040. Per material segment the out-of-time Gini is 0.694 for CS1 and 0.726 for CS2, 0.731 for credit lines, 0.689 for term loans and 0.668 for business mortgages, and per grade the realised default rates increase monotonically from R01 to R12. On reference dates under the current definition of default (December 2020 to December 2024) the Gini is 0.711, so risk differentiation is also demonstrated on data reflecting the current definition. The model has good predictive power, its drivers are plausible and no material bias was found in the calibration tests of section 7.2, so its use does not distort own funds requirements.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and analysis of individual defaults
sections.text: Calibration was tested per pool and per calibration segment with one-sided binomial and Jeffreys tests of the pool PD before MoC against the realised long-run default rate: no pool has a p-value below 5% and the lowest p-value is 0.08 (R11, CS1). For each of the 52 quarterly calculation dates the average PD before MoC of each segment was compared with the one-year default rate and with the LRA; the one-year rates fall within the range expected under the hybrid philosophy, and the ratio of average PD to one-year default rate lies between 0.60 and 1.72. On the out-of-time sample the realised default rate (1.46%) is below the average best-estimate PD (1.83%), consistent with the benign conditions of 2023–2025, and the Hosmer–Lemeshow test on best-estimate PDs rescaled to the out-of-time default rate does not reject calibration (p = 0.27). The back-testing uses the full history of 52 reference dates, and its methods and data are documented in the monitoring plan and will be updated at least annually. Because defaults in the best grades are few, all 214 defaults in grades R01–R04 of the out-of-time sample were analysed individually with SME Credit Risk Management: 48 followed the loss of a major customer, 31 the death or illness of the owner, 23 fraud and the remainder sudden liquidity events. The main drivers of these defaults are not observable in the data before default, and the model was not adapted to these singular events; the fraud cases were passed to the fraud risk function.

sections.heading: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of grades
sections.text: Heterogeneity between adjacent grades was tested with one-sided tests of the difference in realised default rates: all adjacent pairs differ significantly at 5% (the weakest pair, R01–R02, with p = 0.04), so no grades had to be merged. Homogeneity within grades was tested by comparing, per grade, the default rates of subsets by calibration segment, legal form, product type, sector group and region with the rest of the grade; no material subset shows a significantly different default rate, except business credit card holders in R08, a subset of 0.4% of the grade's exposure. The distributions of the best-estimate PDs of adjacent grades do not overlap significantly by construction of the master-scale boundaries, and exposures within each grade are sufficiently homogeneous. Risk differentiation is demonstrated on the time series of realised default rates per grade over good and bad years, including the 2012–2013 recession and the 2020–2021 support period, with monotonic grade default rates in every year.

sections.heading: Stability
sections.text: Stability across time was demonstrated on quarterly cohorts of the out-of-time sample (Gini between 0.692 and 0.724) and across segments (section 7.1). Re-training with five random seeds gave out-of-time Gini values between 0.707 and 0.711 with a standard deviation of 0.15 percentage points, below the limit of one percentage point for Tier 1 models, and 99.1% of obligors kept the same grade. Perturbing each hyperparameter by one step of the search grid changed the out-of-time Gini by at most 0.6 percentage points. The rank correlation of global SHAP importances between the out-of-sample and out-of-time samples is 0.94 for the 27 features.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger comparison
sections.text: The model was compared with an interpretable challenger, the logistic regression with weight-of-evidence binning re-estimated on the same RDS and target (out-of-time Gini 0.664), and with version 1.3 in production (0.638); the uplift of 4.5 percentage points over the challenger exceeds the two-point threshold of AI-STD-700 §10.3. The differences arise mainly among obligors with rising utilisation but stable arrears, where the challenger underestimates risk, and in the tails (R01–R02 and R11–R12), where gradient boosting separates better; the challenger does not outperform the model on any material metric. As an external benchmark the bureau's own default probability class was compared with the model grades on the out-of-time sample: the bureau score reaches a Gini of 0.58, the rank correlation with the model PD is 0.61, and grade-level default rates of the model are consistent with the bureau classes. The Bank's supervisory benchmarking submission includes the SME retail portfolio, and the results for 2025 showed average PDs within the interquartile range of peers.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses covered the key assumptions, parameters and input data: alternative exclusions (including EX-02 to EX-04: LRA −0.01 percentage points), alternative target definitions (UTP-only defaults excluded: Gini +0.4 points, LRA −0.31 points), alternative calibration windows (2016–2025 only: LRA 1.76%) and alternative expert judgements (EJ-SME-04 to EJ-SME-06). The results and their effect on the output are documented in Annex 7.B and support the quantification of the MoC components in chapter 6, for example the calibration window sensitivity for MOC-SME-B2. For each material expert judgement the effect was tested under reasonable alternatives: removing the monotonic constraints (EJ-SME-04) lowers the out-of-time Gini by 0.2 points but produces three non-monotonic relationships; one instead of two calibration segments (EJ-SME-05) raises CS2 PDs by 14%; and AA-01 without adjustment (EJ-SME-06) lowers the LRA by 3.7%. Robustness to plausible data errors was tested by perturbing each continuous feature by ±5% and by setting single features to missing: 1.8% of obligors change grade under the ±5% perturbation, and the largest effect of a missing feature (bureau_payment_index) is a PD increase of 7% on average.

sections.heading: Explainability
sections.text: The explainability, fairness and robustness analyses required by AI-STD-700 are summarised in sections 7.7 and 7.8 and documented in full in the explainability and fairness report EVD-04-XAI v1.0. Global explanations use TreeSHAP values computed on the out-of-time sample: the ten most important features by mean absolute SHAP value are max_dpd_12m (18.2% of the total), util_ratio_avg_6m (12.6%), bureau_payment_index (10.9%), inflow_trend_12m (8.4%), overdraft_excess_months_6m (7.1%), business_age_years (5.2%), equity_ratio (4.8%), returned_debits_6m (4.5%), balance_volatility_12m (4.1%) and rel_length_months (3.6%), and their dependence plots confirm the expected business relationships. Local SHAP values are computed for every production prediction and stored with it, and the five largest positive contributions are translated into ranked reason codes mapped to 31 standard statements reviewed by SME Credit Risk Management for comprehensibility. SHAP additivity holds within 1e-9 for all out-of-time predictions, and explanations are stable for similar inputs. The explainability techniques, the evaluation dimensions (fidelity, stability, comprehensibility), the limits of the explanations (for example the split of attributions between correlated features) and the explainability needs of credit officers, clients, validators and supervisors are documented in EVD-04-XAI. The purpose, logic, main inputs, limitations and intended use of the model are described for users in the model user guide.

sections.heading: Fairness and robustness
sections.text: Fairness was tested before approval on the out-of-time sample for sole proprietors and partners, whose sex and age group are lawfully available from customer due diligence records and were used only in a separate access-restricted fairness dataset. With a favourable outcome defined as a grade of R08 or better, the ratio of favourable-outcome rates between the least and most favoured group is 0.96 for sex and 0.84 for age group (lowest for owners under 30), above the threshold of 0.80. The difference in true-positive rates between groups is 1.2 percentage points for sex and 3.9 percentage points for age group, below five points, and calibration by group shows realised-to-predicted default ratios between 0.91 and 1.07. No fairness threshold is breached, so no root-cause analysis or AI Governance Office approval for retention was required; fairness will be retested at every periodic review, and the results are documented here and in EVD-04-XAI. Accuracy and robustness are demonstrated by the performance, stability and perturbation tests of sections 7.1 to 7.6, drift is covered by the monitoring plan, and cybersecurity risks such as data poisoning and model extraction were assessed with Information Security (EVD-04-XAI section 12).

sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions, each assessed for plausibility, are: (1) the relationships between the features and default learned on 2012–2022 remain stable, supported by the out-of-time and cohort results; (2) the quality and definitions of behavioural and bureau data remain stable, supported by the data quality controls and monitoring; (3) the adjusted LRA is representative of the long-run default experience; (4) the portfolio composition remains within the range of the RDS; and (5) the model is used only for monthly behavioural rating within the range of application. The model does not work effectively for obligors with a relationship shorter than six months (out-of-time Gini 0.52), for sectors with fewer than 500 observations (mining, energy supply), for obligors near the EUR 1 million threshold with corporate-like risk profiles, and in shocks outside the range of the RDS such as a recession deeper than 2012–2013.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: The handover to implementation on 18 November 2026 included the implementation specification IS-MDL04-v2.0, the trained model artefact (LightGBM model file with SHA-256 hash), the calibration and MoC parameter tables, the feature caps table, 2,400 test cases and reference outputs produced with the development code on the full out-of-time sample. The implementation specification is consistent with this MDD, was approved by the model owner on 25 November 2026 before implementation started, and defines every transformation, missing-value and outlier treatment, calibration formula, parameter, master scale mapping, floor and override rule with precision and rounding conventions. Implementation testing, record-level reconciliation, the parallel run and user acceptance testing are documented in the implementation and testing report EVD-04-IMPL v1.0. This MDD, the RDS documentation, the implementation specification and the production code are consistent with each other; the consistency check of March 2027 found one open item, recorded in EVD-04-IMPL, which is resolved in the release before go-live.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan: KPIs and thresholds
sections.text: The monitoring plan, approved by the model owner on 26 March 2027 and submitted to Model Validation for review, defines the following KPIs with calculation, thresholds, frequency, data, segments, responsible persons and escalation per traffic light, and forms chapter 10 of this MDD. KPIs cover: PSI of the score, the grade distribution and the ten most important features against the development sample (green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25); Gini on the latest outcome window compared with development (relative decline above 10% amber, above 20% red, and red below 0.50 regardless of change); calibration per grade and portfolio with the one-sided Jeffreys test (portfolio p below 5% or more than 20% of grades amber, p below 1% or more than 30% of grades red); override rates by direction (amber above 5%, red above 10%); production data quality; and model coverage. KPIs are computed for the portfolio, each calibration segment and each grade. Monitoring is performed quarterly, calibration KPIs annually, and fairness metrics and explanation drift semi-annually; results are finalised and reported within 60 calendar days after the reference period. The model is static: parameters are not updated in production, so no dynamic ML component requires monitoring of changes in model logic between releases.

sections.heading: Escalation, actions and reporting
sections.text: Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use, with changes processed under MRM-STD-050; red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the MRC. A red monitoring outcome, or an annual review concluding that estimates are inadequate, leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the MRC within three months. The quarterly monitoring report shows each KPI with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over at least the last four cycles; the override rates by direction, reason, magnitude and approving unit with the realised performance of overridden versus non-overridden cases; and the model coverage, including obligors with missing or outdated ratings. The monthly SME credit risk report to senior management shows the risk profile by grade, migration across grades, the PD per grade and the comparison of realised default rates with the PDs and with stress-test outcomes. The annual rating system report to the MRC covers the materiality of the rating system, its perceived strengths and limitations and its status in the light of validation and audit actions. Monitoring results are sent to SME Credit Risk Management, which uses the model in credit decisions, and the monitoring code and data are version controlled so that results are reproducible.

sections.heading: Annual review of estimates
sections.text: The estimates are reviewed when new information comes to light and at least annually in the annual review of estimates, whose framework defines the minimum scope, the metrics and thresholds of section 10.1 and the predefined actions of section 10.2. The review analyses the representativeness of the RDS against the application portfolio, including structural breaks; the performance and stability of the model per period on the whole application portfolio without development exclusions; and predictive power, including whether the latest year of data changes the LRA materially and back-testing per grade against realised default rates. It also covers the adequacy of the MoC, the need for recalibration, the monitoring results, changes in portfolio and environment, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and code-documentation consistency, and concludes, with the sign-off of the model owner, whether the model remains fit for purpose; the review including the comparison of realised default rates with the estimates is submitted to Model Risk Management and Model Validation. Quantitative methods and data are kept consistent through time, and any change of method or data source or period is documented in the review. Each review extends the data window with the latest year so that data under the current definition of default gradually replace the approximated period.

sections.heading: Retraining governance
sections.text: Retraining is not automatic: the model is retrained only on a trigger (red discriminatory power or input drift not explained by portfolio changes, or a planned redevelopment) or in the three-yearly model review; the data window is the full RDS extended with the latest reference dates. Retraining may change the tree parameters, and within the documented search space the hyperparameters, while keeping the feature set, target and algorithm; a retrained version must pass acceptance tests on out-of-time Gini (no decline above two points), seed stability, monotonicity, fairness thresholds and grade migration (below 10% of exposures moving more than one grade). Every retraining is classified under MRM-STD-050, and continuous or online learning is not used in production.

sections.heading: Expert judgement
sections.text: All expert judgements are recorded in the expert judgement log EJ-SME log v1.4, stored with the model documentation: EJ-SME-01 to 03 in data treatment (RDS section 6.3), EJ-SME-04 constraint directions (low), EJ-SME-05 two calibration segments (medium), EJ-SME-06 appropriate adjustment AA-01 (medium, LRA +3.8%) and EJ-SME-07 cap of business age at ten years (low). Each judgement in model design is justified in this MDD (sections 2.3, 4.5 and 5.1), and each log entry states the assessment criteria, rationale, evidence, assumptions, experts involved, alternatives rejected, quantified impact, proposer, approver, approval date and review date. Materiality follows MRM-STD-023 §4: medium judgements were challenged by T. Kuipers and approved by the model owner and the head of SME Credit Risk Modelling, low judgements by the model owner, and no proposer approved his or her own judgement. The aggregate effect of all expert judgements on the portfolio average final PD is +4.6% and 3.1% of exposures change grade, below the high-materiality threshold, so no MRC approval of the aggregate is required; all judgements were approved before the affected output is used. No MoC is quantified by expert judgement: all MoC components are based on sensitivity analysis. The rationale of each judgement is specific enough for a third party to replicate its effect.

sections.heading: Explainability approach and stakeholder needs
sections.text: The Bank's standard attribution method is SHAP; for the tree ensemble the exact TreeSHAP algorithm (shap 0.45.0, interventional perturbation with a background sample of 10,000 development observations) is used, which yields contributions in log-odds that add up to the model score. The explainability needs of four stakeholder groups were collected in interviews in October 2026: credit officers need the main drivers of an individual grade in business language; clients need the main reasons for a credit decision on request; validators need global and local attributions and dependence plots; and supervisors need evidence that the drivers are economically plausible. The explanations are evaluated on three dimensions with criteria: fidelity (additivity within 1e-6 and agreement with permutation importance), stability (rank correlation of attributions for similar inputs above 0.9) and comprehensibility (review of reason code statements by SME Credit Risk Management). Known weaknesses and limits of the explanations are the split of attribution between correlated features (for example utilisation and overdraft excess), the dependence of interventional SHAP values on the background sample, and the fact that SHAP values explain the model and not causal effects; these limits are stated in the user guide. The level of explanation is proportionate to the impact of the use case: global explanations for governance and validation, and individual explanations for every grade used in a credit decision, available to the staff acting on it.

sections.heading: Global feature importance
sections.text: Global importance was computed as the mean absolute SHAP value per feature on the out-of-time sample: max_dpd_12m 18.2%, util_ratio_avg_6m 12.6%, bureau_payment_index 10.9%, inflow_trend_12m 8.4%, overdraft_excess_months_6m 7.1%, business_age_years 5.2%, equity_ratio 4.8%, returned_debits_6m 4.5%, balance_volatility_12m 4.1% and rel_length_months 3.6%; the remaining 17 features together account for 20.6%. The ranking agrees with the credit experts' expectations: arrears history, liquidity usage and payment behaviour dominate, followed by business maturity and financial strength, which is consistent with the early-warning indicators used by SME Credit Risk Management. Permutation importance on the same sample gives the same top five features in the same order, and the Spearman rank correlation between SHAP and permutation importance over all 27 features is 0.93.

sections.heading: Dependence, monotonicity and plausibility
sections.text: SHAP dependence plots were produced for the ten most important features, showing the relationship between each feature value and its contribution to the score across all predictions: risk rises steeply with days past due up to 60 days and flattens thereafter, rises with utilisation above 80% of the limit, and falls with the bureau payment index, credit turnover trend, business age and equity ratio. Compliance with the monotonic constraints was verified with partial dependence and ICE curves on the out-of-time sample: the partial dependence of all 19 constrained features is monotonic in the documented direction. ICE curves of individual obligors show no violations beyond numerical tolerance, except for util_ratio_avg_6m, where 0.3% of the curves decrease slightly between utilisation of 0.95 and 1.05; this was attributed to the interaction with overdraft_excess_months_6m and assessed as immaterial (maximum PD effect 0.02 percentage points). The learned relationships of the eight unconstrained features are plausible: for example the sector risk group ranks construction, hospitality and retail as the riskiest groups, in line with the sector default rates of the RDS.

sections.heading: Local explanations
sections.text: Local SHAP values are computed for every prediction in the monthly production run, and because the model is Tier 1 and drives decisions on individual clients, the 27 local SHAP values of each production prediction are stored with the prediction in the rating history table for the retention period of the ratings. Credit officers see, for each obligor, the grade, the PD and a waterfall of the five largest contributions in the credit workstation, so individual explanations are available to all staff acting on the output. Local explanations were reviewed for a stratified sample of 300 obligors across grades by three credit officers, who judged the main drivers plausible in 291 cases; the nine remaining cases concerned recent limit changes whose effect credit officers expected to be larger.

sections.heading: Reason codes
sections.text: Because grades lead to credit decisions reviewed by credit officers and communicated to clients, the model produces ranked reason codes: the five features with the largest positive SHAP contributions are mapped to 31 standard statements, such as "payments on the account were more than 30 days overdue in the last 12 months" or "credit turnover on the business account has declined". The mapping table (reason_codes_v2.0.csv) is documented in the implementation specification and was reviewed for comprehensibility by SME Credit Risk Management and the client communication team in November 2026.

sections.heading: Fidelity and stability of explanations
sections.text: SHAP additivity was tested on all 865,672 out-of-time predictions: the sum of the SHAP values and the expected value reproduces the model log-odds with a maximum absolute difference of 8e-10. Stability for similar inputs was tested on 20,000 pairs of obligors that differ by less than 1% in every continuous feature and are identical in categorical features: the Spearman rank correlation of their SHAP vectors has a median of 0.97, and the top reason code is identical in 94.8% of the pairs. Recomputing the SHAP values with a second background sample changed the ranking of the ten most important features in one position (ranks 9 and 10 swapped).

sections.heading: Missing values and explanations
sections.text: Structurally missing values are handled by the default split direction learned by LightGBM; for sole proprietors without annual accounts the missing equity_ratio receives on average a SHAP contribution of +0.04 log-odds, close to the contribution of an equity ratio of 10%, which is plausible for small unincorporated businesses. For clients with a relationship shorter than six months the behavioural features are missing and their combined contribution is on average +0.21 log-odds; reason codes for these clients state that limited account history is available, which supports the manual review of these clients in grades R09–R12 (limitation LIM-04).

sections.heading: Fairness testing: data and method
sections.text: Fairness was tested before approval for all obligors that are natural persons (sole proprietors and partners, 63% of obligors), covering sex and age group (under 30, 30–49, 50–64, 65 and over), which are lawfully available from customer due diligence records; other protected attributes are not available and are not collected for this purpose. The protected attributes are kept in a separate fairness dataset in the secure analytics environment, accessible only to two named members of the fairness testing team and not used for any other purpose; no special categories of personal data are processed. The favourable outcome is defined as a grade of R08 or better, which corresponds to the automated acceptance zone of the credit acceptance process; true-positive rates are measured as the share of non-defaulting obligors that receive a favourable outcome. Tests are repeated on the out-of-sample test sample and per calibration segment to check the stability of the results.

sections.heading: Fairness results
sections.text: The adverse impact ratio between the least and most favoured group is 0.96 for sex (women versus men) and 0.84 for age group (under 30 versus 50–64), both above the threshold of 0.80. The difference in true-positive rates is 1.2 percentage points between sexes and 3.9 percentage points between the age groups under 30 and 50–64, below the threshold of five points. Calibration by group is reported: the ratio of realised to predicted default rates ranges from 0.91 (65 and over) to 1.07 (under 30), and from 0.97 (men) to 1.02 (women). sections.heading: Proxy screening
sections.text: All 27 features were screened for proxy effects by predicting each protected attribute from each feature (univariate AUC and Cramér's V): all features stay below the AUC of 0.65 and Cramér's V of 0.30 except business_age_years, which predicts owner age under 30 with an AUC of 0.71. Business age is retained with a documented credit-risk rationale (business maturity is an established driver of SME default independent of the owner's age, and 22% of businesses under two years old have owners over 40) and is capped at ten years to limit its use to the minimum needed; the AI Governance Office approved the retention on 17 September 2026 (AIGO-2026-044). A multivariate screen (gradient boosting on all 27 features predicting each protected attribute) reached an AUC of 0.58 for sex and 0.74 for age group; removing business_age_years lowered the latter to 0.66 but reduced the model Gini by 0.9 percentage points.

sections.heading: Robustness and security
sections.text: Robustness was tested by perturbing each continuous input by ±5% and ±10%: under ±5% 1.8% of obligors and under ±10% 4.1% of obligors change grade, mostly by one grade; setting single features to missing changes the PD by at most 7% on average (bureau_payment_index). Resilience against data drift is covered by the PSI monitoring of the score and the ten most important features, and against errors by the production data quality checks that stop the rating run for red DQ results. Information Security assessed the risks of data poisoning, model extraction and model inversion on 11 February 2027: training data come only from controlled internal sources and a contracted bureau, the model artefact and scores are accessible only to authorised systems and staff, and reason codes do not expose model parameters; the residual risk was assessed as low.

sections.heading: Human oversight and instructions for use
sections.text: Human oversight is assigned to credit officers, who review the grade, PD and reason codes in each credit decision and may override within policy SME-OVR-2026, and to SME Credit Risk Management, which approves overrides, monitors the model and can stop its use by reverting to version 1.3 through the fallback procedure. The criteria for intervention are defined in the user guide: reason codes that contradict recent information about the client, grades inconsistent with known events not in the data, and clients with limited history in grades R09–R12. The model user guide UG-MDL04-v2.0 provides the instructions for use to internal users: intended purpose, range of application, known limitations, performance levels per segment, interpretation of reason codes and the expected oversight tasks.

sections.heading: AI literacy and training
sections.text: The developers, the validators assigned to MDL-04, the use case owner and the credit officers assigned to human oversight complete the role-specific AI training of the Bank before assignment to the use case, with refresher training every two years; by 28 February 2027, 214 of 226 credit officers in the SME acceptance and account management teams had completed the module 'AI-supported credit rating'. The module covers the functioning of gradient boosting at a conceptual level, the interpretation of SHAP-based reason codes, the limits of the explanations and the override policy, taking into account the staff's technical knowledge and the context of use.

sections.heading: Record-keeping
sections.text: The rating engine automatically records for every production run the run identifier, reference date, input data version, code and parameter version, and for every prediction the inputs, score, PD, grade, SHAP values, reason codes and any override, enabling traceability of the system's functioning over its lifetime. The logs are written to the rating history database, which users of the credit workstation cannot alter.

sections.heading: Scope and approach
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the reference data set RDS-SME-PD-2026.1 for PD Retail SME version 2.0, performed before development and before the RDS freeze, in accordance with MRM-STD-022 and DATA-POL-001 §8.1. sections.heading: Critical data elements and DQ rules
sections.text: For every critical data element at least one DQ rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension, 164 rules in total, and where a dimension is not applicable the reason is recorded (for example timeliness is not applicable to static registration data such as the incorporation date). The rules are documented in Annex 1 of this report, which forms part of the RDS documentation, and the 131 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool under rule set DQ-MDL04. Each rule is assigned to exactly one dimension so that results can be aggregated per dimension: completeness 58 rules, accuracy 21, consistency 39, timeliness 14, validity 26 and uniqueness 6.

sections.heading: Thresholds
sections.text: Each rule has an amber and a red threshold at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3 (completeness below 98% amber and below 95% red, reconciliation differences above 0.5% amber and above 1% red, logical consistency below 99% amber and below 98% red, timeliness one and three months beyond the required refresh). For the default flag, default date and default trigger stricter thresholds apply (completeness 100%, consistency above 99.9%), at least as strict as the defaults. One deviation was approved: the completeness threshold of turnover of sole proprietors for 2012–2014 is set at 85% amber and 80% red because the data are missing at source for these years; the deviation is justified in the RDS documentation (deficiency DD-02), was approved by the model owner and, being less strict for a Tier 1 model, by Model Risk Management on 5 June 2026.

All material risk data of the portfolio are captured, across all products, legal forms, sectors and regions of the Dutch business banking entity.

sections.heading: Accuracy and reconciliation
sections.text: Accuracy was measured by reconciling outstanding balances, limits and arrears amounts per reference date with the general ledger and the product systems: the absolute difference in outstanding balance is below 0.1% on all reference dates, and record counts agree exactly after the documented exclusions. Critical data elements are reconciled at least annually against the source systems or accounting data, and no unexplained differences were found in the 2026 reconciliation; any unexplained difference would be recorded as a data quality issue. The exposures in the RDS reconcile with the EAD reported in COREP for the retail SME class at the 2024 and 2025 year-end reference dates within 0.2%, the difference being explained by off-balance items outside the model scope, so the model data are reconcilable with the regulatory reports. Checks operate from data entry to reporting: the source systems validate data at entry, the Risk Data Warehouse reconciles each load with the source totals, and the RDS build reconciles with the warehouse.

sections.heading: Data quality framework, ownership and reporting
sections.text: The assessment applies the Bank's data quality management framework formalised in DATA-POL-001 and MRM-STD-022, which covers all data used in IRB processes, including the external bureau data. Ownership of data quality is defined for business and IT: the Data Owners of the five data domains are accountable for data quality at source, the Risk Data Warehouse team for the integration layers, and SME Credit Risk Modelling for the RDS. It defines every input variable with its production source field and lineage, every transformation, missing-value and outlier treatment, the calibration formula and parameters, the pool boundaries and master scale mapping, the MoC factors, the PD floor and the override rules, with a precision of eight decimals for PDs and rounding only at reporting. It includes 2,400 test cases with expected outputs produced by the development code, covering typical cases in every grade and calibration segment, boundary values at each pool boundary, missing and invalid inputs and every legal form and product type.

sections.heading: Test results and defects
sections.text: All 2,400 test cases were executed; 2,396 passed at first execution and four failed because of defects, which were resolved and retested before sign-off: DEF-01 wrong handling of a negative equity ratio below the cap, DEF-02 reason code text truncation, DEF-03 rounding of PDs to six instead of eight decimals and DEF-04 missing-value handling for a new product code. DEF-01, DEF-03 and DEF-04 affected model outputs and were resolved in release 2.0.1, so no defect affecting model outputs remains open; the test plan, cases, results and defect log are stored in the test management tool.

sections.heading: Record-level reconciliation
sections.text: Production outputs were reconciled at record level with the outputs of the development code on identical input data covering the full out-of-time sample (865,672 records) and the three parallel-run reference dates. After release 2.0.1 the maximum absolute PD difference is 3e-9 and the pool and grade assignment is identical for all records, within the tolerances of 10^-6 absolute for continuous outputs and identity for categorical outputs. The differences outside tolerance observed before release 2.0.1 were all explained by DEF-03 and DEF-04, and no unexplained difference remains.

sections.heading: Parallel run
sections.text: A parallel run of version 2.0 alongside version 1.3 was performed for three monthly reference dates, 31 December 2026, 31 January 2027 and 28 February 2027, covering a full production cycle including the quarterly COREP run, before any use of version 2.0 for decisions or regulatory reporting. At 28 February 2027, 65.2% of exposures keep their grade, 28.7% move by one or two grades and 6.1% by more than two grades; the portfolio average final PD rises from 2.41% to 2.52% and the RWEA of the range of application from EUR 2.43 billion to EUR 2.52 billion (+3.7%). Operational issues were limited to the late bureau delivery on 31 January 2027, handled by the documented fallback to the previous delivery for 1,210 obligors.

documents.title: Model change memorandum PD Retail SME v2

sections.heading: Change description and rationale
sections.text: The change replaces the logistic regression behavioural scorecard of PD Retail SME version 1.3 by a gradient boosting classifier with monotonic constraints and SHAP-based explanations (version 2.0), introduces two calibration segments, extends the calibration data to 52 quarterly reference dates up to December 2024, and recalibrates the pool PDs and the margin of conservatism. The objective is to improve risk differentiation, which had declined for version 1.3 to an out-of-time Gini of 0.638, and to address the 2024 validation finding on the use of transaction data; the planned implementation date is the first month-end at least one month after the ECB permission, expected in the second half of 2028. The affected range of application is the retail SME exposure class of the Dutch business banking entity: 108,960 obligors, 146,300 facilities, EAD EUR 6.12 billion and RWEA EUR 2.41 billion at 30 June 2026. The change was recorded in the change log of the model inventory on 6 October 2025 (change CHG-MDL04-2025-01), before any implementation in production.

sections.heading: Affected components and documents
sections.text: Affected components are the risk differentiation function, the grade assignment, the calibration, the MoC and the override policy; the definition of default, the master scale, the range of application and the PD floor are unchanged. Affected documents are the RDS documentation (EVD-04-RDS v1.0), the MDD (EVD-04-MDD v1.0), the explainability and fairness report (EVD-04-XAI v1.0), the implementation specification IS-MDL04-v2.0, the implementation and testing report (EVD-04-IMPL v1.0), the override policy SME-OVR-2026 and the model user guide. The data sources for grade assignment change: current account transaction aggregates from the Payments Data Hub and bureau dispute counts are new inputs, and the calibration time series is extended beyond the annual inclusion of the latest observations; both are included in this application rather than notified separately.

sections.heading: Internal materiality
sections.text: Every change is classified by internal materiality and regulatory class; this change is internally material because it alters the methodology and the risk drivers and introduces new material input sources, irrespective of its output impact. The impact on aggregate output at 30 June 2026 is +4.6% on the portfolio average final PD and +3.8% on RWEA, and 34.8% of exposures change grade, exceeding the 10% threshold for grade assignments of MRM-STD-050 §5.2(e).

sections.heading: Regulatory classification
sections.text: Under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 the change is classified as material (Class A), requiring prior permission under CRR Art. 143(3), because it changes the fundamental methodology for estimating PD, including the MoC methodology (Annex I, Part II, Section 1, point 2(f)), and the switch from a traditional to a mostly ML-based approach is a material model change under the ECB guide to internal models. The quantitative criteria are not met, because RWEA increases (+3.8% for the range of application and +0.21% of the Bank's credit and dilution risk RWEA), but the qualitative criteria alone determine Class A. Where the classification is in doubt the higher category is applied under the Bank's change policy, which sets detailed criteria to ensure consistent and arbitrage-free classification; in this case no doubt exists. Because the change is material, it does not qualify as a non-material methodology change for ex ante notification.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 6.2 sets MOC-SME-A1 at the upper end (+4.0% CS1, +3.6% CS2) of three alternative approximations of the 2012–2015 default flag. Model Validation's independent sensitivity analysis adds a plausible alternative not considered by the developers, namely a UTP proxy based on the transfer to special management at 60 days past due combined with a reconstructed three-month probation period, which raises the LRA by +6.3% (CS1) and +5.7% (CS2). The applied Category A MoC is therefore lower than the adverse effect of the plausible range, and the total MoC of CS1 would rise to 19.7%, close to the 20% redevelopment trigger of CRM-STD-101 §7.2.

mitigation.text: Extend the sensitivity analysis of MOC-SME-A1 with the special-management UTP proxy, set the Category A MoC at no less than the resulting adverse effect (or obtain MRM approval of a justified lower value), and present the updated total MoC to the MRC together with the assessment under CRM-STD-101 §7.2.

deficiencies.rationale: RDS sections 5.1 and 5.1.1 demonstrate representativeness on risk-driver distributions and on default-rate levels by calibration segment, legal form, product, sector and grade. Model Validation's representativeness test by business age shows that start-ups (businesses younger than two years, 9.4% of current obligors against 6.1% in the RDS) have a realised one-year default rate at 30 June 2025 of 4.1% against 3.1% in the RDS for the same score bands (+32% relative, significant at 1%), a red result under MV-HB-003 §6.3 that the segment splits used by the developers do not reveal.

mitigation.text: Add business age as a dimension of the default-rate representativeness analysis, assess the calibration of the start-up segment, and either apply an appropriate adjustment or a Category B MoC for start-ups, or justify that the difference is transitory, before approval by the MRC.

deficiencies.rationale: The LRA before MoC is not compared with a reference LRA over the best-practice period 2008–2018 because internal data start in 2012. The comparison with the 2012–2018 sub-period (2.61%) shows a higher value than the adjusted LRA (2.16%), and the justification given (credit policy changes and benign recent years) is qualitative and not supported by an analysis of the missing 2008–2011 years.

mitigation.text: Construct a reference LRA for 2008–2018 using available proxies (for example default rates of the version 1 scorecard population or macro-based back-casting with the MDL-10 satellite model), quantify the difference with the adjusted LRA and either justify it quantitatively or revise the LRA or MoC.

deficiencies.rationale: For 7.8% of legal-entity observations the financial statements used as risk drivers are older than 24 months. The documentation states that the model uses the age of the statements as a feature instead of an explicit conservative adjustment in the assignment process; it is not demonstrated that the learned effect is conservative for outdated statements.

mitigation.text: Introduce an explicit conservative treatment of financial statements older than 24 months in the assignment process (for example a one-grade downgrade or treatment of financial features as missing), or demonstrate with realised default rates that the learned effect of fin_stmt_age_months is adequately conservative.

deficiencies.rationale: The use case is classified as high-risk under Annex III point 5(b). The fundamental rights impact assessment required before first use is only planned for the third quarter of 2027 and has not been coordinated with DPIA-2026-061 yet; the documentation does not evidence its content.

mitigation.text: Complete the fundamental rights impact assessment, coordinated with an updated DPIA, and obtain the AI Governance Committee use-case approval before version 2.0 is used for credit decisions on natural persons.

validationTests.detail: RDS independently rebuilt from the source snapshots of 12 June 2026 with Model Validation's own extraction: 5,184,298 observations (−14, −0.0003%) and 104,209 default observations (−6); all differences traced to late-registered party merges. Key-variable distributions identical (PSI < 0.001).

Code-versus-documentation review of sme-pd-gbm v2.0.0: util_ratio_avg_6m is unconstrained in the trained artefact (monotone_constraints = 0) although MDD section 4.5 documents an increasing constraint; ICE analysis by Model Validation shows non-monotonic behaviour for 0.3% of obligors. All other parameters (hyperparameters, caps, calibration, MoC, floor) match the MDD.
Re-training with five seeds and perturbed hyperparameters (learning rate ±0.01, leaves ±4): out-of-time Gini 0.703–0.712, standard deviation 0.3 percentage points (green, threshold 2 points).

Two-sample tests of default-rate levels by business age: start-ups younger than two years show a realised one-year default rate of 4.1% at 30 June 2025 against 3.1% in the RDS for the same score bands (+32% relative, p < 0.01) – red. Other segments by legal form, product and sector are green.

The MoC for data deficiencies is supported by sensitivity analyses (MOC-SME-A1 to A3, B1, B2), but Model Validation's own sensitivity analysis of DD-01 with a special-management UTP proxy gives +6.3% (CS1) against the applied +4.0%; MOC-SME-A2 and A3 are confirmed.
